meet-your-faculty.html
Meet Your Faculty TA’s

Meet Your Faculty Trevor Pugh (He/Him) Senior Scientist, Princess Margaret Cancer Centre Director, Genomics, Ontario Institute for Cancer Research Toronto, ON, Canada trevor.pugh@utoronto.ca Dr. Trevor Pugh, PhD, FACMG is a cancer genomics researcher and board-certified molecular geneticist at the forefront of precision medicine. As holder of the Canada Research Chair in Translational Genomics, he uses genome sequencing to understand causes of cancer, guide treatment of patients, and detect early disease using blood tests. He directs the OICR Genomics Program and the Princess Margaret Genomics Centre; genomics cores that specialize in single cell, cell-free DNA and clinically-accredited whole genome sequencing. He has contributed to multiple large-scale genomics and data-sharing programs including The Cancer Genome Atlas, NCI TARGET, AACR GENIE, and the Terry Fox Marathon of Hope Cancer Centres Network. He leads the CHARM Consortium, an initiative to use cell-free DNA monitoring for all people with an inherited predisposition to cancer. Originally from Vancouver, Dr. Pugh received a PhD in Medical Genetics from the University of British Columbia and was an early student of the Canadian Bioinformatics Workshop. Linda Xiang (She/Her) Data Scientist II Ontario Institute of Cancer Research Toronto, ON, Canada lxiang@oicr.on.ca Linda is a Senior Data Scientist with over a decade of experience designing and delivering production-grade data platforms for large-scale international genomics initiatives, including ICGC/ICGC-ARGO, PCAWG, GDC, and VirusSeq. Her work focuses on bridging complex scientific requirements with robust engineering solutions, spanning bioinformatics workflow architecture, data services, and platform integration. She has led the development of containerized, reproducible pipelines for genomic data processing and submission across cloud and on-premises environments, and has driven the adoption of standards-based frameworks to improve scalability and maintainability. In parallel, she has led the design of interoperable clinical and genomic data models to support secure data sharing and federated analysis, while contributing to global standards development through GA4GH. Yoshiaki Tanaka (He/Him) Associate Professor Centre de Recherche de l’Hôpital Maisonneuve-Rosemont, Université de Montréal Montreal, QC, Canada yoshiaki.tanaka@umontreal.ca Dr. Yoshiaki Tanaka obtained his undergraduate degree (2006) in pharmaceutical science at Tokyo University of Science, Japan. During his Ph.D. training (2006-2011), he pursued purely bioinformatics approaches using large-scale datasets, such as RNA-seq and ChIP-seq, to model the relationship between transcriptional and epigenetic regulation in eukaryotic cells under the supervision of Dr. Kenta Nakai at University of Tokyo, Japan. He also applied machine learning algorithms to high-throughput sequencing data to investigate chromatin conformation regulations. For his post-doctoral studies, Tanaka joined Dr. In-Hyun Park laboratory at Yale University USA (2011-2020) to seek out complementary training in cell and molecular biology with the goal of understanding stem cell pluripotency and tissue development. Recently, he developed in vitro 3D models of human brain and elucidated mechanistic insight of brain development and neuronal diseases. Dr. Tanaka’s research vision at Maisonneuve-Rosemont Hospital Research Center (CRHMR), University of Montreal is to explore complex problems related to brain tumor and other neuronal diseases using both in vitro and in silico modeling. Robert Eveleigh Senior Bioinformatics Specialist Canacian Centre for Computational Genomics (C3G), McGill University Montral, QC, Canada > Robert Eveleigh, MSc, is a Senior Bioinformatics Specialist at the Canadian Centre for Computational Genomics (C3G) at McGill University. For about 15 years he has developed variant detection pipelines in GenPipes, with a focus on DNA alterations, and he has benchmarked each new sequencing instrument brought into the centre. He develops SOPs for benchmarking to determine the optimal steps for germline and somatic alteration detection. He led development of the GenPipes tumor-pair pipeline, which has processed over 5000 patients, including hundreds from PROFYLE (Precision Oncology for Young People). He is first author of a 2026 Genome Biology paper benchmarking sequencing technologies for variant detection. Mathieu Lajoie Research Associate - Bioinformatician Rosalind and Morris Goodman Cancer Institute, McGill University Montreal, QC, Canada Mathieu Lajoie is a Research Associate and Bioinformatician in Dr. Ian Watson’s laboratory at the Rosalind and Morris Goodman Cancer Institute, McGill University. He holds a PhD in Bioinformatics from Université de Montréal and has more than 10 years of experience in cancer research. He has worked on a wide range of computational biology topics, from algorithm development to regulatory genomics and tumour evolution. His current research focuses on melanoma, integrating genomic and spatial transcriptomic data to investigate disease progression and therapeutic response. Vida Talebian Bioinformatician Ontario Institute for Cancer Research Toronto,ON,Canada Vida is a bioinformatician at the Diagnostic Development program at OICR. She holds a master’s degree in bioinformatics from the University of Waterloo with a computer engineering background. She is involved in projects with a focus on analyzing and integrating multi-omics data to identify prognostic signatures in clinical studies. Aqsa Alam (She/Her) Bioinformatician III Ontario Institute for Cancer Research Toronto,ON,Canada aalam@oicr.on.ca Aqsa Alam is a bioinformatician in the Clinical Genome Interpretation team at the Ontario Institute of Cancer Research. Aqsa did her Honours BSc with high distinction in Biology and Physics at the University of Toronto Mississauga and her MSc in Cell and Systems Biology at the University of Toronto. Aqsa is passionate about communication and scientific outreach. Her current work focuses on genomic interpretation in cancer and supporting accredited clinical trials. Veronique Voisin Computational Biologist Princess Margaret Center Toronto,ON,Canada veronique.voisin@gmail.com Véronique Voisin, PhD, is a computational biologist affiliated with the Princess Margaret Cancer Centre (UHN), where she works with Dr. Aaron Schimmer, SickKids, where she works with Dr. Grace Egan, and the University of Toronto, where she continues to collaborate with Dr. Gary Bader. She uses bioinformatics tools to analyze omics and clinical data and untangle biological questions relevant to leukemia and cancer treatment. Her work includes pathway and network analysis of gene expression data using tools such as GSEA and Cytoscape. She has also contributed to bioinformatics training through the Canadian Bioinformatics Workshop (CBW) over several years. Ruth Isserlin Research Data Analyst The Donnelly Centre, University of Toronto Toronto,ON,Canada ruth.isseerlin@utoronto.ca Bioinformatician and data analyst in the Bader lab applying pathway and data analysis to varied data types. Developed Enrichment Map App for Cytoscape, an app to visually translate functional enrichment results from popular enrichment tools like GSEA to networks. Further developed the Enrichment Map Pipeline including development of additional Apps to help summarize and analyze resulting Enrichment Maps, including PostAnalysis, WordCloud, and AutoAnnotate App. Nicholas Geoffrion Senior Bioinformatician, Infrastructre Manager Meta Platform for Integrated Genomics, Azrieli Reasearch Center, CHU Sainte-Justine Montréal, QC, Canada nicholas.geoffrion.hsj@ssss.gouv.qc.ca Nicholas Geoffrion is a bioinformatician and Genomics Platform Infrastructure Manager at the Azrieli Research Centre in Montréal, specializing in long-read sequencing, computational genomics, and translational cancer research. His work focuses on integrating emerging sequencing technologies, particularly Oxford Nanopore, with scalable bioinformatics pipelines and high-performance computing infrastructure to support genomic research and clinical applications, with a particular emphasis on pediatric oncology. His interests span software engineering, infrastructure automation, open-source technologies, and the development of computational tools that make genomic analysis faster, more accessible, and clinically actionable. TA’s Oliver De Sa Bioinformatician III Ontario Institute for Cancer Research Toronto,ON,Canada odesa@oicr.on.ca Oliver De Sa is a bioinformatician in the Window-of-Opportunity (WOO) network at the Ontario Institute for Cancer Research. Oliver completed a BSc in Biochemistry, followed by an MSc in Immunology both at the University of Toronto. His current work focuses on multi-omic analyses for WOO clinical trials, integrating various data types to describe the molecular mechanisms through which the tumour microenvironment responds to treatment. Module 2 Understanding and Visualizing Data Lecture Lab

Module 2 Understanding and Visualizing Data Lecture Lab In this lab, we’ll demo a popular tool and resources related to exploring our data and potentially finding datasets of interest. The only requirements for the tutorial are as follows: An internet connection A modern browser An account with COSMIC : https://cancer.sanger.ac.uk/cosmic/register Learning Objectives How to use IGV browser to explore data types : BAMs, VCFs, BEDs How to browse and make use of the visualization functions in cBioPortal How to browse and make use of the visualization functions in COSMIC Part 1 - IGV Learning Objectives How to use IGV browser to explore data types : BAMs, VCFs, BEDs How to traverse the genome Loading Tracks and annotations How to find additional info for each genomic feature To get started, Please navigate over to https://igv.org/app/ Question : Aside from avoiding installation issues, a browser version is much more convenient and accessible. Why should one consider using a local installation of IGV vs the online version? Data size - Imagine streaming multiple 500 GB files Data protection - if you’re working with sensitive data that is under DACO restriction or patient data, you’re limited by where you store and send the data BAM Step 1 – Open IGV-Web and choose the genome Make sure our build is on Hg38, to do so click “Genome” and navigate the dropdown to find GRCh38/hg38 Let’s load our data, select Tracks, then URL from the dropdown, Step 2 – Loading the BAM and Index Paste the following info, ensure the BAM file goes into the Track and index file into index: https://42basepairs.com/download/s3/gatk-test-data/wgs_bam/NA12878_20k_hg38/NA12878.bam https://42basepairs.com/download/s3/gatk-test-data/wgs_bam/NA12878_20k_hg38/NA12878.bai NA12878 is the GIAB/1000 Genomes reference individual. This BAM is a very small subset of a whole-genome run: about 61,000 mapped reads across the whole genome, compared with hundreds of millions in a real 30× genome. It is meant for teaching. Step 3 – Post loading sanity check What do we see after loading? Question : We don’t see much. How come? One possibility is wrong genome build. Not the case here but a possibility. The toy BAM being examined is also very small in comparison. So the reads representation will be sparse. In both the browser and local version of IGV, the number of reads visualized is limited, especially at whole genome view that’s an overwhelming amount of data to visualize. For the browser, imagine everyone trying to load a 1TB BAM. Local version can adjust settings according to hardware limitations. Step 4 – Zoomed in look Let’s zoom in to a more manageable view. Paste the following coordinates into the search bar chr1:143,220,111-143,221,807 Once the result loads, what do we see? Question : What are the grey lines? What do the ends (sharp vs blunt) represent? Each grey bar is a read. The pointed end shows the direction it was sequenced: pointing right = forward (+) strand, pointing left = reverse (−). Question : What are the colour dashes in each block? Mismatches Question : What is the graph bar above? Coverage, the height represents the amount of reads per BP. If coloured, shows the ratio of mismatches per nucleotide Step 5 – Read features Clicking on a read, its info can be displayed. Question : What do the blue, red and orange reads represent? When compared to the grey reads, the reads are identified due to their abnormal insert size. The causes could vary from a genomic feature (e.g. structural variant), RNA-seq (though not in this case), lack of size selection during library prep (there would be other signs as well). Toggleable via the gear icon on the right side of the track. Select under “Color by”, “Pair Orientation & insert size (TLEN)” Step 6 – Utilizing track annotations Let’s try a different region chr2:32,915,196-32,917,755 Question : Why are almost all reads coloured? Similarly to the last question, the reads are highlighted due to the unexpected read orientation. What genes are these reads at? How would we find out? - RefSeq is already loaded. We can try another annotation We can see that the reads intersect a “lncRNA” (long non-coding RNA). VCF Step 7 – Working with VCFs (Germline SNVs) Let’s load a VCF https://42basepairs.com/download/web/giab/data_somatic/HG008/NIST/HG008-T_bulk/20240508p100/analysis/GRCh38/BCM_Revio_HG008T-p100_20260313/HG008-T_vs_HG008-N-P/small_variants/HG008-N-P.dipcall.germline.vcf.gz https://42basepairs.com/download/web/giab/data_somatic/HG008/NIST/HG008-T_bulk/20240508p100/analysis/GRCh38/BCM_Revio_HG008T-p100_20260313/HG008-T_vs_HG008-N-P/small_variants/HG008-N-P.dipcall.germline.vcf.gz.tbi These VCFs come from HG008, the GIAB pancreatic cancer tumour/normal cell-line pair, and not from NA12878. The BAM and VCFs belong to different people, so don’t expect the reads to support these variants. Then navigate to the coordinates : chr1:143,206,141-143,206,141 Let’s note what we see: Focusing on the non-greyed feature, what are the VCF features? A G 30 . END=89177 GT:AD 1/1:0,2 chr1 143206141 . A G 30 . TRF;END=143206141 GT:AD 0/1:70,2 Question : What type of variant is it? SNP according to the “type” Question : What are the feature’s coordinates? Can be found under “LOC” Question : What is the reference vs alt? “REF” represents the sequence found in the reference genome. “ALT” represents the sequence that was found in the sample. In this case it was a “A” vs “G” thus the SNP Also take note of the genotype in IGV : “A|G”. This notation is different than in the VCF and carries some different interpretations. In VCFs the genotype field can present as `0/1` meaning unphased or `0|1` phased. Being phased means we know which allele belongs on which chromosome copy. The same cannot be said for unphased. Short read sequencing does not provide that resolution, and would need long reads (for example). That context is lost in IGV, and instead IGV displays the alleles as bases, e.g. A|G, using `|` as a fixed separator regardless of phasing. Question : What is the depth? “AD” stands for allelic depth and represents the evidence/reads supporting each allele. It’s interpreted by the genotype “A | G” and “70,2” meaning 70 reads support the reference and 2 reads support the alt allele. Question : Compared to the features beside it, why are those features greyed out? Other SNPs were filtered. For the specific reason, see the “FILTER” section. Definitions for the filter are likely to be found within the header of the VCF file. It is a structural variant. Much larger than the single base of SNVs. The Alt also indicates it is a deletion event. Question : How long is the feature? ~10.8 Mb according to the SV length field Question : What is the feature’s ID and what purpose does the ID field serve? “severus_DEL3275” and to act as a unique identifier Question : How would we find out how many genes are affected by the feature? The BCFtools Consequence or BCSQ identifies the genes affected. BED/bigBed Step 9 – Working with BigBed / External Annotation Let’s explore BED files. Load the following URL into the track https://hgdownload.soe.ucsc.edu/gbdb/hg38/encode4/ccre/encodeCcreRegistry.bb Question : Notice anything different with the file suffix? It is a bigBed file. The same as a regular bed file but binarized, compressed and indexed for accessibility. IGV is able to only fetch the region on screen and does not require a separate index file. To find out more see the following link How to interpret the features described by the bed file? The UCSC genome browser describes the file in great detail, specifically: For more info see the following link If we navigate to TP53 by typing TP53 in the search bar, we see the following: TP53 has 26 RefSeq transcripts, but IGV only shows 2 of them. We can access the settings on refSeq annotation through the gear on the right → Set track height → 700. All 26 rows appear. Question : What is the red feature? What is the importance of the feature and where it is located? It is a promoter-like element (PLS). ENCODE only assigns this class to regions near an annotated transcription start site. The main TP53 promoter is the cluster of red elements at the far right (~7,687 kb). The single red element at ~7,676.7 kb sits inside the full-length gene, in intron 1, just upstream of exon 2, which holds the start codon. Its promoter-like chromatin and a GENCODE V39 transcript starting there suggest a candidate alternative start site. Part 2 - cBioPortal Learning Objectives How to browse and make use of the visualization functions in cBioPortal Learn to query genes and datasets of interest Make use of visualizations to discover relationships and biological trends Firstly, what is cBioPortal? As per their about page, Multimodal data represented in interactive visualizations that facilitates biological discovery and clinical decisions. It incorporates patient-level cohort data such as mutations and clinical data. Step 1 – Select the studies and build the query Navigate to https://www.cBioPortal.org/ and select the following two studies: - Breast Cancer (METABRIC, Nature 2012 & Nature Commun 2016) - Consists of 2,509 samples of targeted sequencing on primary tumours with 549 normal matched - Breast Invasive Carcinoma (TCGA, PanCancer Atlas) - 1,084 samples as part of a large cohort that profiled 10,000 tumours across 33 cancer types Click “query by gene” at the footer and query the following : TP53 PIK3CA BRCA1 BRCA2 PTEN STK11 CDH1 PALB2 CHEK2 ATM BARD1 RAD51C RAD51D FGFR2 TOX3 MAP3K1 ESR1 ERBB2 GATA3 These genes are commonly altered in breast cancer, and working with them in the tutorial will provide some insight of their significance. Step 2 – OncoPrint We are presented with an OncoPrint Question : What do the first four rows present and mean? As indicated in the legend, the first four rows provide info on donors’ membership in the respective datasets and whether they were profiled for copy number changes, mutations, and structural variants. Question : We see multiple genes, focusing on TP53 and PIK3CA, what can we infer? The percentage represents the number of donors with genetic alterations, where the legend specifies the type and proportion of donors Step 3 – Cancer Types Summary On the above tabs, navigate to the cancer types summary view Question : What does the barchart summarize for us? X-axis gives info on the dataset and included profiled genomic alteration types. The Bars provide a frequency of genomic alterations. Step 4 – Mutual Exclusivity Moving on to mutual exclusivity, select significant only and sort by q-value starting with lowest/most significant The first row denotes TP53 and ERBB2. Question : What does the finding of co-occurrence entail? Based on the two datasets, TP53 and ERBB2 are often both found to be altered Perhaps an interesting link to look at Looking at the second row of TP53 and CDH1 Question : What does the finding of mutual exclusivity entail? Very few examples exist in the two breast cancer datasets where both TP53 and CDH1 co-occur, in fact most donors have one or the other. This could signify a dependency specific to the cancer type. Step 5 – Plots Exploring the plots tab next. Let’s use the quick filter for FGA vs Dx Question : What info can we glean from the plot? The TCGA datasets are split up into various types of breast carcinomas. Breast invasive ductal carcinoma shows the highest fraction of genome altered, signifying genomic instability. Let’s look at the mutations tab, specifically for gene TP53 Step 6 – Mutations Let’s look at the mutation with the highest donor count Question : Where does it occur in TP53? In the TP53 region that binds DNA. Amino acid 248 Question : What type of mutation is it? Different types, but often missense Question : Are there any Post-Translational Modifications associated with the mutation? On the left, we can add annotation tracks. Specifically we’re interested in Post-Translational Modifications (PTM). Scrolling around, no modification coincides with the mutation. Speaking of annotations, what if we wanted to find out more about the mutation? What can we look up through OncoKB? Hovering over the first row of the mutations table, note the record of sample ID MB-0211 with the protein change R248Q Hover on the dartboard icon under the column annotation Step 7 – Comparison/Survival Looking at survival curves. Question : What can we understand about TP53 vs unaffected cohort (no alteration in any of the 19 queried genes)? Patients with TP53 mutations initially have poorer survival odds but around 180-200 months have better outcomes compared to the unaffected cohort. Step 8 – CN Segments Lastly, let’s look at copy number segments which brings us back to IGV. Looking at PIK3CA vs TP53 Question : what differences do we observe? TP53 mutations are copy number losses while PIK3CA mutations are copy number gains. Part 3 - COSMIC COSMIC (Catalogue of Somatic Mutations in Cancer) is a curated knowledge base of somatic mutations drawn from the literature and large-scale studies, along with data from other assays (e.g., methylation) and analyses (e.g., drug resistance). An example use-case would be exploration with cBioPortal to find trends and patterns followed up with validation and annotating significance in COSMIC. Learning Objectives How to browse and make use of the visualization functions in COSMIC Navigate datasets by refining the search using visualization functions Navigate to COSMIC. You’ll need an account to access the data. Follow the prompts at the following link : https://cancer.sanger.ac.uk/cosmic/register Step 1 – Search for a gene Search for TP53 in the header search bar Additionally, ensure you’re on the correct genome build GRCh38. The search returns the results page which groups hits by type (Genes, Mutations, Samples, Cancers, etc.). We need to choose the gene TP53 to open the gene page. Step 2 – Read the gene view The central gene view plot displays various types of info along the length of the gene. Hovering on the top substitution, we’ll find the position to be 273. We can further zoom in to that region for more info. Step 3 – Zoom to positions 270–275 Apply the filters on the left-hand side for 270-275. The result is the following barchart of substitutions. Question : Which substitution is the most common at position 273 of the TP53 gene? p.R273H (c.818G>A) 1551 Step 4 – Open the mutation page Clicking on the mutation brings us to a page dedicated to the mutation. Here, a number of interesting things can be viewed, including samples with the mutation, related references, and pathways. - The shape is the same (missense hotspots in the DNA-binding domain plus truncations everywhere), but COSMIC’s top hotspot is R273 across all cancers, while in cBioPortal’s two breast cohorts it was R248, with R175 and R273 close behind - Different sample collections give different rankings of the most common mutation! We can also observe the tissue type distribution of samples with the TP53 mutations. Step 5 – Jump to a tissue: the Cancer Browser Clicking on the Large Intestine brings us to a page dedicated to Large Intestine. Step 6 – Back to TP53 with the tissue filter We can then see the top genes mutated in Large intestinal samples. Clicking the TP53 mutation returns us to the TP53 page but with additional filters. Note the left-hand filter with tissue type selection applied. The result is that the most represented mutation is now different. Previously it was 3908 at position 273 but the most frequent mutation is now 175 with 1069 mutation count. We can observe how different tissue types reflect different mutations. Part 4 - Advanced Exercises Exercise 1 – Real genome or alignment artefact? (Part 1, BAM) Go back to the two regions you looked at in NA12878.bam: Region 1: chr1:143,220,111-143,221,807 Region 2: chr2:32,915,196-32,917,755 Do the reads in these regions reflect the actual genome of the sample, or are they mostly alignment artefacts? What in the IGV view supports your answer? To help you decide, add two annotation tracks. Open Tracks → Hosted Annotations…, go to Mapping and Sequencing, and tick: LowMap+SegDup (under Difficult regions from GIAB). GIAB uses this track to mark segmental duplications and regions that are hard to map with short reads. Simple Repeats (under Repeats). In region 1 you should see one bar over the whole window, with the repeat unit TCGAATGGAATCATCA. Does what you see in these tracks change or confirm your answer? Answer Both regions are mostly alignment artefacts. In region 1, most reads are drawn transparent, which means mapping quality 0, and each read has several mismatches. The few coloured pairs (red, blue, orange) also have MAPQ 0, and their mates are far away on chr1 or on chr14. LowMap+SegDup covers the whole window. This part of chr1 exists in several nearly identical copies, so reads that really come from another copy end up here, and the small differences between the copies show up as mismatches. In region 2, the reads are short and heavily clipped, and almost every one has a different colour because the mates are spread over many chromosomes. Most of them are supplementary alignments with MAPQ 0. The reference sequence bar is solid orange, which is a run of about 400 G’s, followed by a block of 1,000 Ns. Low-quality, G-rich pieces of unrelated reads stick to this run of G’s. Low mapping quality, evidence that doesn’t agree (mates scattered everywhere), and a repeat or duplication underneath are the typical signs of an artefact. A real variant or SV would be supported by many well-mapped, independent reads telling the same story. Exercise 2 – TP53 in the germline VCF (Part 1, germline VCF) HG008 is a pancreatic cancer patient. The germline variants in this file come from long-read (PacBio HiFi) sequencing of the patient’s normal tissue. The variants were called with dipcall, which builds the two chromosome copies from the long reads and compares each one with the reference. As you go through the variant and genotype fields, look out for what the long reads add that you would not usually get from short reads. Go to TP53 (chr17:7,668,000-7,690,000). Click the variant at chr17:7,676,154, then click its genotype cell. Go through every field in both popups and write down what you think each one means. Is this variant germline or somatic? How can you tell? Answer Germline. The variant is in the normal sample (HG008N), so the person was born with it. It is rs1042522 (Use the annotation ClinVar dbSNP under Variation), the well-known TP53 Pro72Arg variant. In most populations the arginine version (the ALT here) is actually the more common one: a “variant” only means different from the reference genome, not rare or harmful. What does 0|1 tell you that 0/1 would not? Answer The pipe means the genotype is phased: we know which chromosome copy carries the ALT allele. This comes from the long reads (HiPhase). Note that IGV shows A | G in the popup either way, so check the PS field to see whether a variant is phased. Find another heterozygous variant in TP53 with the same PS value. Is its ALT allele on the same chromosome copy as the ALT at 7,676,154? Answer All heterozygous variants in TP53 share PS 7498016, so they belong to one phase block. Variants written the same way (0|1) have their ALT on the same copy; a 1|0 variant has its ALT on the other copy. Why is AD only 1,1 for this variant? Answer This VCF was made by dipcall, which compares two genome assemblies with the reference rather than counting reads. Here AD counts assembly pieces, one per chromosome copy, so a heterozygous site shows 1,1 and a homozygous one 0,2. For the same reason, QUAL is always 30. Which fields in this VCF would you not expect to see in a germline VCF made from short reads? Answer The main addition from the long reads is phasing. Most heterozygous genotypes are written with a pipe (0|1), and the PS (phase set) and PF (phasing flag) fields record which phase block each variant belongs to. Phase blocks here are tens of kilobases long, so a whole gene like TP53 sits in one block. With short reads, most variants would be unphased (0/1) and these fields would be missing. Some other fields come from how this particular file was made rather than from the read length: dipcall compares two genome assemblies with the reference, so AD counts assembly pieces, QUAL is always 30, and the filters (HET1/2, GAP1/2) describe problems with the assemblies. A short-read caller would instead give read counts (AD, DP) and genotype quality (GQ). Exercise 3 – KRAS and CDKN2A in the somatic SV VCF (Part 1, somatic VCF) HG008 is a pancreatic cancer. The tumour and normal samples were sequenced with long reads. The SV variants are called by the long-read structural-variant caller Severusa which compared the tumour and normal to find SVs present only in the tumour. The resulting file contains the two classic pancreatic cancer events: a gain of the oncogene KRAS and a loss of the tumour suppressor CDKN2A. Gene Locus SV record KRAS chr12:24,600,000-26,850,000 severus_DUP1372 CDKN2A chr9:21,940,000-21,985,000 severus_DEL7384 For each one, click the SV and its genotype cell, and note SVTYPE, SVLEN, STRANDS, the genes listed in BCSQ, VAF, DR/DV and HP. Why would a tumour gain an extra copy of an oncogene but lose a tumour suppressor? Answer KRAS sits in a 1.95 Mb tandem duplication that covers 12 genes (VAF 0.36, HP 1). An extra copy of an oncogene increases its growth signal. CDKN2A is removed by a 19.9 kb deletion (VAF 1, DR 0, DV 11, HP 1). Losing a tumour suppressor removes a brake on cell division. Oncogenes help a tumour when they become more active, and tumour suppressors help it when they are lost. The CDKN2A deletion has genotype 0/1, yet its VAF is 1. What could explain this? Answer A VAF of 1 means none of the reads at the breakpoints show the normal sequence, so there is most likely no intact copy left: the other copy was probably lost by a separate event. CDKN2A is completely inactivated in this tumour. Somatic genotypes are only approximate, and VAF is more informative. Since HG008-T is a cell line, there are no normal cells to lower the VAF. What does the field STRANDS with the value -+ tell you about the KRAS event? Answer -+ describes a junction that faces outward, which is the signature of a tandem duplication. With short reads, the same event shows up as read pairs facing away from each other. Exercise 4 – cBioPortal (Part 2) BRCA1 and BRCA2 are the best-known breast cancer genes, yet in the OncoPrint they are altered in only 3–4 % of patients. Why? Answer BRCA1 and BRCA2 are famous because inherited (germline) variants in them strongly raise cancer risk. The TCGA and METABRIC data in cBioPortal are somatic, meaning only changes found in the tumour, so germline variants are not shown. Germline BRCA1/2 carriers account for only about 5 % of breast cancers. BRCA1 can also be switched off by promoter methylation or by losing one copy, and neither counts as “altered” by default. How often a gene is mutated in tumours is not the same as how important it is for cancer risk. Summarise in one sentence what each view is useful for: OncoPrint, Cancer Types Summary, Mutual Exclusivity, Plots, Mutations, Comparison/Survival and CN Segments. Answer View Useful for OncoPrint Seeing which patients have which alterations, across all queried genes at once Cancer Types Summary Comparing alteration frequency between studies or cancer types Mutual Exclusivity Testing whether two genes tend to be altered together or rarely together Plots Comparing any two attributes, for example fraction of genome altered by subtype Mutations Seeing where mutations fall on the protein (hotspots vs spread out) and their annotation Comparison/Survival Checking whether altered and unaltered patients differ in survival or clinical features CN Segments Looking at copy-number gains and losses along the genome, in an embedded IGV Exercise 5 – COSMIC (Part 3) What is COSMIC, and how is it different from cBioPortal? Answer COSMIC, the Catalogue Of Somatic Mutations In Cancer, is run by the Wellcome Sanger Institute. Its team collects somatic mutations from thousands of published papers and genome screens, across all cancer types. cBioPortal is organised around studies: you pick a cohort and see each patient’s alterations together with clinical data such as survival. COSMIC is organised around genes and mutations: you ask how often a particular mutation has been reported, and in which tissues. COSMIC is free for academic use after registration; cBioPortal is open. What are other COSMIC features worth a look? Answer A few worth further exploring: the Cancer Gene Census (a curated list of cancer genes and their role), Mutational Signatures (patterns that point to causes such as smoking or UV light), the Cancer Mutation Census (mutations ranked by evidence that they drive cancer), COSMIC-3D (mutations on protein structures), Actionability (links to drugs and clinical trials) and the Cell Lines Project. Exercise 6 – Which tool for which question? Which tool would you use to answer each of these questions? Is this variant real in my sequencing data? What do the reads look like? Answer IGV It shows your own reads, with mapping quality, mismatches and read pairs How often is a gene altered in a cohort, with which other genes, and does it affect survival? Answer cBioPortal It combines cohort data with clinical outcomes Has this exact variant been seen before, in which tissues, and what papers report it? Answer COSMIC It collects somatic mutations from published studies, by tissue Is this variant clinically actionable? Answer OncoKB (or CIViC) Experts link variants to approved drugs and trials. OncoKB annotations also appear in cBioPortal Is this variant common in healthy people (likely benign germline)? Answer gnomAD It gives allele frequencies from hundreds of thousands of people In practice these tools are often used together: IGV to check that a variant is real, gnomAD to check that it is rare, COSMIC and cBioPortal to see whether it is known in cancer, and OncoKB to see whether it matters for treatment.

Module 3 Genome Alignment Lecture Lab 1. Purpose We will practice genomic alignment tool, BWA, and post-alignment tool, Picard and SAMtools, with whole genome sequencing data. 2. Dataset SRX4728544: Whole Genome Sequencing of CRL-2324 breast cancer cell line Due to huge size of the original data, please use the following small datasets. * SRR7890824_10M_1.fastq.gz * SRR7890824_10M_2.fastq.gz Tang et al., Establishing community reference samples, data and call sets for benchmarking cancer mutation detection using whole-genome sequencing, Nat Biotechnol. 2021 Sep;39(9):1151-1160. doi: 10.1038/s41587-021-00993-6. Epub 2021 Sep 9 3. Workflow 1.Download human referecne genome wget https://hgdownload.gi.ucsc.edu/goldenPath/hg38/bigZips/hg38.fa.gz Indexing human reference genome. This process may takes 1 hour. bwa index hg38.fa.gz Check output ls bwa index will generate the following five files. hg38.fa.gz.amb hg38.fa.gz.ann hg38.fa.gz.bwt hg38.fa.gz.pac hg38.fa.gz.sa Perform genomic alignment bwa mem hg38.fa.gz SRR7890824_10M_1.fastq.gz SRR7890824_10M_2.fastq.gz -t 4 > SRR7890824_10M.sam If more multithreds are available, increase number of -t option. For example, -t 8. Add RG (read group information) for subsequent analytic tools and convert SAM format to BAM format. picard AddOrReplaceReadGroups \ INPUT=SRR7890824_10M.sam \ OUTPUT=SRR7890824_10M.rg.bam \ RGID=group1 \ RGLB=lib1 \ RGPL=ILLUMINA \ RGPU=unit1 \ RGSM=sample1 \ VALIDATION_STRINGENCY=LENIENT Sort BAM file picard SortSam \ INPUT=SRR7890824_10M.rg.bam \ OUTPUT=SRR7890824_10M.sorted.bam \ SORT_ORDER=coordinate \ VALIDATION_STRINGENCY=SILENT Mark duplicate picard MarkDuplicates \ INPUT=SRR7890824_10M.sorted.bam \ OUTPUT=SRR7890824_10M.dedup.bam \ METRICS_FILE=metrics.txt` Make BAM index samtools index SRR7890824_10M.dedup.bam Finally, you will obtain the following BAM and BAM index files. SRR7890824_10M.dedup.bam SRR7890824_10M.dedup.bam.bai
