This is the tumor depth ratio we plot. referenceGCDiploidRatio Normal ratio, further normalised so a normal diploid region is 1 (accounts for the sex chromosomes) referenceGCContent, tumorGCContent GC content of the reads in the window value -1 Window not used (N bases, low mappability, extreme GC) # **`cobalt.ratio.pcf`**: same layout as the AMBER pcf. Here `mean` is a **log2** ratio: use `2^mean` to get back to the ratio scale. peek(file.path(cobalt_dir, paste0(tour_sample, ".cobalt.ratio.pcf"))) # **`<normal>.cobalt.ratio.median.tsv`**: one line per chromosome. Look at chrX (\~0.5: only one X) and chr16 (\~0.57: part of chr16 is lost in the normal itself). read_tsv(file.path(cobalt_dir, "SPP_GT_0-1_1.cobalt.ratio.median.tsv"), show_col_types = FALSE) %>% filter(chromosome %in% c("chr1", "chr6", "chr16", "chr19", "chrX", "chrY")) cobalt.gc.median.tsv: two blocks. The first gives the sample’s mean and median depth; the second the median depth for each GC percentage. It is important to account for GC bias, as sequencing read counts can vary substantially across regions with different GC content. Depth is not constant across GC content: in the normal it drops from about 116 (25% GC) to about 90 (60% GC), and both samples lose depth below ~25% GC. If this bias were not removed, GC-rich and GC-poor regions would look like losses or gains. COBALT divides each window’s depth by the median of its GC bucket (this curve), so the tumorGCRatio / referenceGCRatio values are free of GC bias. # The file has 3 header lines (#sampleMean/sampleMedian, their values, #gcBucket/median); # skip all 3 and force numeric columns, otherwise the "#gcBucket" line is read as data # and both columns become text (ggplot then draws no line). read_gc_median <- function(path) { read_tsv(path, skip = 3, col_names = c("gcBucket", "median"), col_types = "dd") } p <- bind_rows( tumor = read_gc_median(file.path(cobalt_dir, paste0(tour_sample, ".cobalt.gc.median.tsv"))), normal = read_gc_median(file.path(cobalt_dir, "SPP_GT_0-1_1.cobalt.gc.median.tsv")), .id = "sample") %>% ggplot(aes(gcBucket, median, colour = sample)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) + labs(x = "GC content of the 1 kb window (%)", y = "Median read depth") + theme_bw() PURPLE: purity, ploidy and copy number File What it is When to use it <tumor>.purple.purity.tsv The best fit: purity, ploidy, sex, status, plus the uncertainty range Report purity/ploidy <tumor>.purple.purity.range.tsv Score of every purity/ploidy combination tested (~16,000 rows) Check whether other solutions are almost as good <tumor>.purple.cnv.somatic.tsv Final copy-number segments (~300 rows) Copy number of any region; genome plots; input for downstream tools <tumor>.purple.cnv.gene.tsv Copy number per gene (~37,000 genes) Is my gene deleted / gained / LOH? <tumor>.purple.segment.tsv All segments before merging (~9,500 rows), with observed and fitted values and the germline status Debug a call: compare observed vs fitted ratio and BAF <tumor>.purple.qc QC summary First thing to check <tumor>.purple.somatic.clonality.tsv Clonality peaks of somatic SNVs Empty here: no somatic VCF (-somatic_vcf) was given plot/*.png PURPLE’s own figures (purity.range, segment, copynumber, map) Quick visual QC plot/<tumor>.somatic_data.tsv Data behind the somatic-variant plots Empty here, same reason purple.version PURPLE version Reproducibility Files that PURPLE can also write but that are missing in this run: purple.driver.catalog.somatic.tsv (needs -driver_gene_panel), the germline files (purple.germline.*, need a matched normal via -reference), and purple.somatic.vcf.gz (needs -somatic_vcf). purple.purity.tsv: one line, the chosen fit (columns explained in the QC section). columns(purple_f(".purple.purity.tsv"), n = 1) purple.purity.range.tsv: every fit that was tried, best first. Column Meaning purity, ploidy The combination tested score How badly it explains the data; lower is better normFactor Scaling between observed ratio and copy number for this fit diploidProportion Fraction of the genome that would be diploid somaticPenalty Penalty from somatic variants (0 without a somatic VCF) read_tsv(purple_f(".purple.purity.range.tsv"), show_col_types = FALSE) %>% head(8) purple.cnv.somatic.tsv: the final segments (columns explained in the PURPLE segments section below). The method column says how the copy number was obtained: method Meaning BAF_WEIGHTED From depth and BAF of the segment itself (most reliable) LONG_ARM Too little data; copied from the rest of the chromosome arm STRUCTURAL_VARIANT, GERMLINE_* Other inference methods (not used in this run) UNKNOWN Could not be inferred cnv_tour <- read_tsv(purple_f(".purple.cnv.somatic.tsv"), show_col_types = FALSE) head(cnv_tour) count(cnv_tour, method) purple.cnv.gene.tsv: one row per gene (columns explained in the Gain, Loss, Deletion and LOH section below). read_tsv(purple_f(".purple.cnv.gene.tsv"), show_col_types = FALSE) %>% filter(gene %in% c("CDKN2A", "MYC", "TP53")) %>% dplyr::select(chromosome, start, end, gene, minCopyNumber, maxCopyNumber, minMinorAlleleCopyNumber, somaticRegions, chromosomeBand) purple.segment.tsv: the most detailed table, useful to understand why PURPLE made a call. Important columns: Column Meaning germlineStatus State of the normal in this segment: DIPLOID (normal), HET_DELETION, HOM_DELETION, AMPLIFICATION, NOISE, CENTROMETIC (sic), EXCLUDED, UNKNOWN observedTumorRatio, observedNormalRatio Measured depth ratios of the segment observedBAF, bafCount Measured (folded) BAF and the number of SNPs tumorCopyNumber, minorAlleleCopyNumber, majorAlleleCopyNumber Copy numbers implied by the chosen purity/ploidy fittedTumorCopyNumber, fittedBAF Nearest whole-number solution and its expected BAF minorAlleleCopyNumberDeviation, majorAlleleCopyNumberDeviation Distance from a whole number: large values = poor fit or subclonal support What defines the segment start: NONE (depth/BAF change), CENTROMERE, TELOMERE, or an SV type if SVs were given segment_tour <- read_tsv(purple_f(".purple.segment.tsv"), show_col_types = FALSE) count(segment_tour, germlineStatus, sort = TRUE) Most segments are DIPLOID in the normal. The HET_DELETION segments are places where the normal has only one copy: mostly large parts of chr6 (~58 Mb) and chr16 (~53 Mb) in this cell line. PURPLE treats these as germline events, so they are not reported as tumor losses. purple.qc peek(purple_f(".purple.qc"), n = 20) Which file answers which question? Question File Column(s) What is the purity and ploidy of my tumor? purple.purity.tsv purity, ploidy How sure is PURPLE about it? purple.purity.range.tsv, plot/*purity.range.png score Did the run pass QC? purple.qc, amber.qc QCStatus What is the copy number of gene X? purple.cnv.gene.tsv minCopyNumber, maxCopyNumber, minMinorAlleleCopyNumber What is the copy number of region chr:start-end? purple.cnv.somatic.tsv copyNumber, major/minorAlleleCopyNumber Is a region LOH? purple.cnv.somatic.tsv (minor CN = 0), confirmed in amber.baf.tsv.gz minorAlleleCopyNumber, tumorBAF Is a change germline or somatic? purple.segment.tsv, normal ratio in cobalt.ratio.tsv.gz germlineStatus, referenceGCDiploidRatio What does the raw evidence look like? cobalt.ratio.tsv.gz, amber.baf.tsv.gz tumorGCRatio, tumorBAF (or use plot_gene() below) Load the files # purity range purple.purity_ranges <- list.files("./Mathieu_purple/purple/plot/", pattern = "purity.range.png", full.names = TRUE) purple.purity_ranges <- normalizePath(sort_by_purity(purple.purity_ranges)) # segment segfiles <- list.files("./Mathieu_purple/purple/plot/", pattern = "segment.png", full.names = TRUE) segfiles <- normalizePath(sort_by_purity(segfiles)) # CN files copyNumberFiles <- list.files("./Mathieu_purple/purple/plot/", pattern = "copynumber.png", full.names = TRUE) copyNumberFiles <- normalizePath(sort_by_purity(copyNumberFiles)) # MAC MAP <- list.files("./Mathieu_purple/purple/plot/", pattern = "map.png", full.names = TRUE) MAP <- normalizePath(sort_by_purity(MAP)) # arrange plots library(png) # readPNG(): read a PNG file into a matrix of pixels library(grid) # rasterGrob(): turn the pixels into a drawable object # combine_pngs(): put several PNG files into one figure, each panel titled # with its sample ID and true purity. Panels are filled row by row. # labels: panel titles; default = sample ID + true purity, "" = no title combine_pngs <- function(files, ncol = 3, labels = NULL, purity = purity_info) { if (is.null(labels)) { ids <- str_extract(basename(files), "SPP_GT_[0-9]+-[0-9]+_[0-9]+") labels <- sprintf("%s (true tDNA fraction %g%%)", ids, 100 * purity[ids]) } panels <- lapply(seq_along(files), function(i) { p <- wrap_elements(full = rasterGrob(readPNG(files[i]), interpolate = TRUE)) # image as a patchwork panel if (nzchar(labels[i])) { p <- p + labs(title = labels[i]) + theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14, hjust = 0.5)) } p }) wrap_plots(panels, ncol = ncol) } All four plots for one sample Change idx to look at another sample (1 = 5% tDNA fraction … 6 = 100% tDNA fraction). idx <- 6 one_sample <- c(purple.purity_ranges[idx], segfiles[idx], copyNumberFiles[idx], MAP[idx]) sid <- str_extract(basename(one_sample[1]), "SPP_GT_[0-9]+-[0-9]+_[0-9]+") # 2 x 2 figure; each PNG already has its own title, so only the sample is labelled (on top) p <- combine_pngs(one_sample, ncol = 2, labels = rep("", 4)) + plot_annotation(title = sprintf("%s (true tDNA fraction %g%%)", sid, 100 * purity_info[[sid]])) & theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 18, hjust = 0.5)) Selection of purity PURPLE tries a grid of purity (y axis) × ploidy (x axis) combinations and gives each one a score: how badly the predicted depth ratio and BAF fit the data (lower is better). In the purity.range.png plots: colours show the score relative to the best fit; blue = within 10% of the best, red = poor; the dashed lines and labels mark the chosen purity and ploidy; several separate blue spots mean several solutions explain the data almost as well (e.g. ploidy 1.4 vs 2.8 at the same purity). This is a common source of errors, because doubling all copy numbers often fits the data equally well. p <- combine_pngs(purple.purity_ranges) What to notice. 100%: one sharp blue spot at purity 99%, ploidy 2.82 (plus a small one at ploidy ~1.4, the “half” solution). 75%: still one clear solution, at the right purity. 50%: two blue spots: the chosen fit (43%, ploidy 2.86) and an alternative at about 73% purity with ploidy ~4.8. PURPLE picked the right one, but the data alone almost allow the other. 20% and below: the blue region is a horizontal band at ~15% purity that stretches over many ploidies: PURPLE cannot tell the ploidy, and it reports about the same purity for all three samples. BAF vs copy number: does the fit explain the data? This plot checks a purity/ploidy fit directly against the data. Observed (coloured density). Each PURPLE segment (from purple.segment.tsv) has: an observed BAF (observedBAF, folded to 0.5-1), and an observed depth ratio (observedTumorRatio), which we turn into a tumor copy number with \[CN = \frac{\text{ratio}\cdot\big(p\cdot\text{ploidy} + (1-p)\cdot 2\big) - (1-p)\cdot 2}{p}\] Segments with many het SNPs count more (the density is weighted by bafCount). Only autosomal segments that are diploid in the normal are used. Expected (black dots). For the same purity p, every allele state “major+minor” (e.g. 2+1) predicts where its segments should fall: \[\text{BAF} = \frac{p\cdot\text{major} + (1-p)}{p\cdot(\text{major}+\text{minor}) + 2(1-p)}, \qquad CN = \text{major}+\text{minor}\] A good fit puts the dense clouds on the black dots. The functions behind the plot (in codes/purple_lab_functions.R): expected_CN(ratio, p, CN_R = ploidy) # depth ratio -> tumor copy number calc_baf(purity, nA = minor, nB = major) # expected BAF of an allele state plot_baf_cn(sample_id, purity = NULL, ploidy = NULL, min_baf_count = 10, max_cn = 8) By default plot_baf_cn() uses PURPLE’s fitted purity and ploidy. With these values, expected_CN() gives back PURPLE’s own tumorCopyNumber. p <- plot_baf_cn("SPP_GT_1-0_1") 100% purity. The clouds sit on whole-number states: a big cloud on 2+0 (copy-neutral LOH), and others on 1+0, 3+0, 4+0, 2+1, 4+1, 2+2. Balanced states (1+1, 2+2) appear slightly right of 0.5: folding a noisy BAF to 0.5-1 always pushes it up a little. p <- plot_baf_cn("SPP_GT_1-1_1") # Test another solution # The purity-range plot of SPP_GT_1-1_1 had a second blue spot at about 73% purity and ploidy 4.8. Give these values to plot_baf_cn() # plot_baf_cn("SPP_GT_1-1_1", purity = 0.73, ploidy =4.8 ) # 4.8 2 50% purity. All states move towards BAF 0.5 because of the normal cells (2+0 is now at BAF ~0.71 instead of 1), but the clouds still sit on the predicted dots. The fit is good. Another solution: The clouds still sit on predicted dots, only every state has one more copy: 2+0 becomes 3+1, 2+1 becomes 3+2, 1+0 becomes 2+1. Both solutions explain the same BAF and depth data, which is why PURPLE found two blue spots. PURPLE prefers the solution with fewer copy-number changes and lower ploidy (here the correct one). Low purity p <- plot_baf_cn("SPP_GT_1-9_1") At 10% purity all expected states are squeezed close to BAF 0.5, and the observed segments form one blurred cloud: many purity/ploidy combinations fit equally badly or well, so the fit cannot be trusted. Try it: run plot_baf_cn() on SPP_GT_3-1_1 with PURPLE’s fit, then with purity = 0.5. How do the dots move relative to the clouds? check specific chromosome p <- plot_chromosome("SPP_GT_1-0_1", "chr1") Segment Each point in segment.png is one copy-number segment, placed at its major (x) and minor (y) allele copy number. Point size = number of BAF points supporting the segment (bigger = more evidence). Colour = how far the segment is from a whole number of copies (blue = close, red = far). In a good fit, most large points sit on integer values (1+1, 2+0, 2+1, …). Points spread between integers suggest the purity/ploidy is wrong or the sample is subclonal. p <- combine_pngs(segfiles) # one figure, panels titled with sample ID and true purity What to notice. At 50-100% purity the large points cluster on whole-number states (1+1, 2+0, 2+1, 2+2, …). At 5-10% purity the points line up along straight lines instead of clusters: with so little tumor signal, PURPLE can place a segment almost anywhere along these lines, so the major/minor split is not determined. Copy number distribution copynumber.png is a histogram of the fitted copy number, weighted by the number of BAF points. Colours split each bar by minor-allele copy number (MACN0 = LOH, MACN1, MACN2). For a good fit the peaks sit on whole numbers. For HCC1395 the largest peak is CN 2 with MACN0, i.e. copy-neutral LOH covers a big part of the genome. p <- combine_pngs(copyNumberFiles) # one figure, panels titled with sample ID and true What to notice. From 50% to 100% purity the histograms look alike: a sharp peak at CN 2 that is almost all MACN0 (copy-neutral LOH), plus peaks at 3 and 4. At 5% and 10% there is almost no MACN0 at all and the copy numbers form a broad, continuous hump between 1.5 and 3.5: the LOH and the integer copy-number states are no longer resolved. MinorAlleleCopy map.png (minor-allele ploidy) is the same idea for the minor allele: a histogram of minor-allele copy number, coloured by total copy number. The bar at 0 is the amount of LOH in the genome. p <- combine_pngs(MAP) # one figure, panels titled with sample ID and true purity What to notice. At 50-100% purity the tallest bar is at minor CN 0: a large part of the genome is LOH. At 20% the LOH is still partly found (bars near 0-0.2). At 5% and 10% the distribution is centred on 1: PURPLE no longer sees the LOH, because the BAF shift it causes is too small (see the expected-signal table in the introduction). Some examples of Gain, Loss, Deletion and LOH <sample>.purple.cnv.gene.tsv summarises the copy number of every gene. A gene can overlap several segments, so PURPLE reports the minimum and maximum. Column Meaning minCopyNumber, maxCopyNumber Lowest / highest copy number over the gene minMinorAlleleCopyNumber Lowest minor-allele copy number (0 = LOH somewhere in the gene) minRegionStart, minRegionEnd Region of the gene with the lowest copy number somaticRegions Number of segments overlapping the gene sample_id <- "SPP_GT_1-0_1" # sample analysed in this section somatic_cnv_gene <- read_tsv(paste0(purple_dir, sample_id, ".purple.cnv.gene.tsv"), show_col_types = FALSE) sample_ploidy <- read_tsv(paste0(purple_dir, sample_id, ".purple.purity.tsv"), show_col_types = FALSE)$ploidy somatic_cnv_gene <- classify_gene_cn(somatic_cnv_gene, ploidy = sample_ploidy) sample_ploidy classify_gene_cn() gives each gene one label, relative to the ploidy of the sample (a gene with 3 copies is a gain in a diploid tumor but normal in a triploid one). Rules, checked in this order: Event Rule Deep deletion min CN < 0.5: no copy left in the tumor Amplification max CN > 3 × ploidy Gain min CN ≥ ploidy + 1 Loss max CN ≤ ploidy − 1 cnLOH minor CN < 0.5 and CN between 1.5 and 2.5 LOH minor CN < 0.5, any other CN Neutral anything else somatic_cnv_gene %>% filter(!chromosome %in% c("chrX", "chrY")) %>% count(event, sort = TRUE) A scatter of all genes: x = highest copy number, y = lowest minor-allele copy number. p <- somatic_cnv_gene %>% filter(!chromosome %in% c("chrX", "chrY")) %>% ggplot(aes(x = maxCopyNumber, y = minMinorAlleleCopyNumber, colour = event)) + geom_jitter(size = 0.6, width = 0.05, height = 0.05, alpha = 0.5) + geom_vline(xintercept = sample_ploidy, linetype = 2) + labs(x = "Max copy number", y = "Min minor-allele copy number", title = paste(sample_id, "- one dot per gene; dashed line = ploidy")) + # bigger, opaque dots in the legend only (the plot keeps small transparent dots) guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 4, alpha = 1))) + theme_bw() Some well-known cancer genes in this sample: genes_of_interest <- c("CDKN2A", "FBXL17", "MYC", "CCND1", "BRCA2", "TP53", "PTEN", "BRCA1", "PIK3CA", "PTPRC") somatic_cnv_gene %>% filter(gene %in% genes_of_interest) %>% dplyr::select(chromosome, gene, minCopyNumber, maxCopyNumber, minMinorAlleleCopyNumber, event) %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 2))) %>% arrange(event) Gene What we see Meaning CDKN2A, FBXL17 CN ≈ 0 Deep (homozygous) deletion: both copies lost. CDKN2A is a classic tumor suppressor. MYC CN ≈ 6, minor 0 Gain of one allele only (6+0) CCND1, BRCA2 CN ≈ 4-5 Gain PTEN, BRCA1 CN ≈ 2, minor 0 Copy-neutral LOH: one allele lost, the other duplicated TP53 CN ≈ 2.8, minor 0 LOH without a change in total copy number relative to ploidy Example: CDKN2A (chr9:21,967,751-21,994,490). Each dot is one gene on chr9; the copy number drops to 0 around CDKN2A. cdkn2a <- c(21967751, 21994490) p_all <- somatic_cnv_gene %>% filter(chromosome == "chr9") %>% ggplot(aes(x = start / 1e6, y = maxCopyNumber)) + geom_point(size = 0.5) + geom_vline(xintercept = cdkn2a / 1e6, linetype = 2, colour = "red3") + labs(x = "chr9 (Mb)", y = "Max CN") + theme_bw() p_zoom <- somatic_cnv_gene %>% filter(chromosome == "chr9", between(start, 21.5e6, 22.5e6)) %>% ggplot(aes(x = start / 1e6, y = maxCopyNumber)) + geom_point() + geom_vline(xintercept = cdkn2a / 1e6, linetype = 2, colour = "red3") + labs(x = "chr9 (Mb), zoom 21.5-22.5", y = "Max CN") + theme_bw() p <- p_all | p_zoom Visualize a gene or a chromosome The figures above each show one signal. To judge a copy-number call, we want all the evidence in one figure. The functions from codes/purple_lab_functions.R draw these tracks (top to bottom): Track Data What to look for Normal ratio COBALT depth of the normal, purple line = segments Should be flat at 1. A change here is germline, not tumor. Tumor ratio COBALT depth of the tumor, red line = segments. Background colour = PURPLE minor-allele CN (beige 0 = LOH, blue 1, lilac 2+, grey = too few SNPs) Steps = changes in total copy number Copy number PURPLE fitted total (black), major (red), minor (blue) CN PURPLE’s interpretation of the two signals Normal BAF AMBER BAF of the normal Always around 0.5 (these SNPs were chosen as heterozygous in the normal) Tumor BAF AMBER BAF of the tumor 0.5 = balanced; two bands = imbalance; 0 and 1 = LOH Genes Selected genes (red) and other genes (grey) Which genes are hit Ref het SNPs per 1 Mb Number of AMBER SNPs per 1 Mb Few SNPs = weak BAF evidence (e.g. centromeres) Red dashed lines mark PURPLE’s lowest-copy-number region within the gene. One gene: plot_gene() plot_gene(sample_id, gene_name, flank = 250e3, show_cn = FALSE) sample_id: e.g. "SPP_GT_1-0_1" gene_name: gene symbol as in purple.cnv.gene.tsv flank: bases shown on each side of the gene (default 250 kb) show_cn: add the PURPLE copy-number track (default FALSE, same layout as Mathieu_purple/plots_gene_region/SPP_GT_1-0_1_chr5_FBXL17.pdf) Deep deletion: FBXL17. The tumor ratio drops to 0 between the red lines (no tumor reads at all) while the normal stays at 1, and there are no BAF points inside: both copies are gone. p <- plot_gene("SPP_GT_1-0_1", "FBXL17") Deep deletion: CDKN2A, now with the copy-number track (show_cn = TRUE): p <- plot_gene("SPP_GT_1-0_1", "CDKN2A", show_cn = TRUE) Copy-neutral LOH: GATA3. The tumor ratio is flat and the copy number is 2, exactly like a normal region, but the tumor BAF is at 0 and 1: one allele was lost and the other duplicated. Depth alone would miss this event; only the BAF reveals it. p <- plot_gene("SPP_GT_1-0_1", "GATA3", flank = 2e6, show_cn = TRUE) One chromosome: plot_chromosome() plot_chromosome(sample_id, chr, genes = NULL, show_cn = TRUE, show_arms = TRUE, baf_lines = TRUE) chr: chromosome name with the chr prefix, e.g. "chr9" genes: optional gene names to mark on the gene track show_arms: top track with the p arm and q arm; the dotted vertical line in every track is the centromere (taken from the PURPLE segment that starts at the centromere) baf_lines: in the tumor BAF track, two dashed lines per PURPLE segment, drawn at b and 1−b so they sit on both BAF bands: black (thick) = mean observed BAF of the segment (observedBAF) orange (thin) = BAF expected for the nearest whole-number state (rounded major+minor) at PURPLE’s purity, as in plot_baf_cn() orange on top of black = the segment fits a whole-number state; separated lines = it does not (noise, subclonal change, or wrong fit). For balanced states (2+2) the black line sits a little away from 0.5: folding a noisy BAF always pushes it outwards. On long regions the 1 kb depth windows are summarised as medians of larger bins, and at most 50,000 BAF points are drawn (the caption says so). p <- plot_chromosome("SPP_GT_1-0_1", "chr9", genes = "CDKN2A") Reading chr9 from left to right: the start of 9p is gained with both alleles (4 copies, 2+2, BAF at 0.5); then comes a long copy-neutral LOH region (2+0, BAF at 0 and 1) that contains the CDKN2A deep deletion; most of 9q has 3 copies (2+1, two BAF bands around 0.33 and 0.67), followed by a second LOH region near the end of the chromosome. Effect of purity on the signal The same deletion (FBXL17) in samples with decreasing purity. Watch the depth ratio inside the deletion and the tumor BAF bands move towards the normal values. for (s in c("SPP_GT_1-0_1", "SPP_GT_1-1_1", "SPP_GT_1-9_1")) { p <- plot_gene(s, "FBXL17") } With the formulas from the introduction (ploidy 2.8; the region around FBXL17 is cnLOH, 2+0): Purity Depth ratio inside the deletion Depth ratio of the neighbours Tumor BAF of the neighbours Tumor BAF inside the deletion 1.0 0 0.71 0 / 1 no SNP reads 0.5 0.41 0.83 0.25 / 0.75 0.5 (only normal reads left) 0.1 0.86 0.96 0.45 / 0.55 0.5 At 50% purity the deletion is still clear: the observed ratio is about 0.52 inside versus 0.87 outside, and the neighbours’ BAF bands sit near 0.28 / 0.72 (close to the table; PURPLE estimated 43% rather than 50% purity for this sample). Inside the deletion the BAF goes back to 0.5 because all remaining reads come from normal cells. At 10% purity the differences are smaller than the noise. Any region: plot_cn_region() For a region that is not a single gene, give the coordinates directly: p <- plot_cn_region("SPP_GT_1-0_1", chr = "chr5", start = 100e6, end = 115e6, genes = c("FBXL17", "APC"), title = "chr5:100-115 Mb") Saving figures save_cn_plot() writes a PDF and a PNG; the height is chosen from the number of tracks. # p <- plot_gene("SPP_GT_1-0_1", "FBXL17") # save_cn_plot(p, "Mathieu_purple/plots_gene_region/SPP_GT_1-0_1_chr5_FBXL17") # # p <- plot_chromosome("SPP_GT_1-0_1", "chr9", genes = "CDKN2A") # save_cn_plot(p, "Mathieu_purple/plots_chromosome/SPP_GT_1-0_1_chr9") Exercises Plot TP53 in SPP_GT_1-0_1 with show_cn = TRUE. Is it LOH, a gain or a loss? How does the tumor BAF support your answer? Pick one gene labelled Gain and one labelled Loss in the table from classify_gene_cn() and plot them. Do the depth ratio and BAF agree with the label? Plot chr17 for SPP_GT_1-0_1 and for SPP_GT_3-1_1 (75%). Which events are still easy to see at 75% purity? Run classify_gene_cn() on SPP_GT_1-1_1 (50%). Is CDKN2A still called a deep deletion? Why might PURPLE’s call change at lower purity? Look at the normal-ratio track of chr16. What do you see, and why does it matter for interpreting the tumor? Plot PTEN with flank = 2e6, show_cn = TRUE. The tumor ratio shows two small focal events right next to the gene (a short gain and a short drop to 0), but the PURPLE copy-number track is flat. Why might PURPLE not call them? (Hint: count the depth windows and BAF points they contain.)

Module 6 Transcriptomics RNA-seq Lecture Lab

Module 6 Transcriptomics RNA-seq Lecture Lab 0. Introduction to the dataset Biological background About 70% of breast cancers are hormone receptor (HR)-positive and HER2-negative. For patients with metastatic disease of this subtype, the standard of care combines endocrine therapy with a CDK4/6 inhibitor. Three such drugs are approved: palbociclib, ribociclib, and abemaciclib. CDK4 and CDK6 drive cells from the G1 phase into the S phase of the cell cycle. They do this by phosphorylating the retinoblastoma protein (Rb). Blocking them arrests tumour cells in G1. Although these drugs prolong progression-free survival, most patients eventually develop resistance. Few treatment options remain after that. The three inhibitors share the same nominal targets, but abemaciclib also inhibits several other kinases. This raises the possibility that tumours become resistant to each drug through different routes. The study The data for this lab comes from: Navarro-Yepes J, Kettner NM, Rao X, et al. Abemaciclib Is Effective in Palbociclib-Resistant Hormone Receptor-Positive Metastatic Breast Cancers. Cancer Research 2023;83(19):3264–3283. PMID: 37384539. RNA-seq data: GEO GSE222367. The authors generated drug-resistant versions of MCF7, a widely used ER-positive/HER2-negative breast cancer cell line. To create abemaciclib-resistant (AR) cells, they cultured several independent pools of MCF7 cells in medium with increasing concentrations of abemaciclib (0.5, 1.0, and 1.5 µM) in a stepwise manner over about 7 months. This produced one resistant line per concentration. Each line was then maintained in medium containing that concentration of the drug. The resistant and parental cells were profiled by RNA sequencing. Thousands of genes were differentially expressed between abemaciclib-resistant and parental cells. Pathway analysis showed that the resistant cells upregulated oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), reactive oxygen species, and lipid metabolism pathways. Consistent with this, they relied on mitochondrial respiration for energy and were sensitive to an OXPHOS inhibitor. In contrast, palbociclib-resistant cells upregulated epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and G2/M pathways and remained sensitive to abemaciclib. Overall, the study concluded that resistance to the two drugs follows distinct transcriptional programs. The samples used in this lab We will compare two groups: Group Sample prefix Description Resistant AR1_MCF7 MCF7 cells resistant to the first abemaciclib dose Control MCF7 Parental, drug-sensitive MCF7 cells Each group includes biological replicates. You will find out how many in the first exercise, using samples.txt. Replicates are essential for the downstream statistical analysis. They allow us to distinguish real expression differences between conditions from normal variation between cultures. The reads are paired-end Illumina sequences. Processing a full human RNA-seq dataset takes hours and a lot of memory. To keep the exercises fast, the data has been reduced to a subset of reads. The reference genome We align the reads to human chromosome 22 only, rather than the full genome. The refs folder contains: chr22.fa: the DNA sequence of chromosome 22 in FASTA format chr22.gtf: the gene annotation for chromosome 22 in GTF format, describing the coordinates of genes, transcripts, and exons Chromosome 22 is one of the smallest human chromosomes, about 51 Mb long and carrying several hundred protein-coding genes. Building an index for it takes minutes instead of hours. Because of this, most reads in the dataset come from other chromosomes and will not align. The gene counts we produce will only cover genes on chromosome 22, so at the of this module when we are doing differential gene expression analysis, you should use the provided full expression dataset. This reference genome was downloaded from ftp.ensembl.org Workflow overview In this lab we take the raw reads all the way to a gene expression table. The scripts provided are for one sample, to practice you will write the scripts for the rest of samples in this dataset for all AR1_MCF7 and MCF7 replicates. Quality control of the raw reads (FastQC) Trimming of adapters and low-quality bases (fastp), with a summary of all QC reports (MultiQC) Reference preparation, building the alignment index (HISAT2, samtools) Alignment of reads to the reference with a splice-aware aligner (HISAT2), followed by sorting and indexing (samtools) Visualization of the alignments (IGV) Gene expression (htseq-count) Differential expression analysis (edgeR) The resulting count tables are the input for differential expression analysis between AR1_MCF7 and MCF7 in the next module. 1. Setting the environment variables An RNA-seq analysis produces many intermediate files: raw reads, trimmed reads, alignments, and expression tables. To keep these organized, we define environment variables that point to a folder for each stage. Commands can then refer to $RNA_ALIGN_DIR instead of a long path. This makes the commands shorter, less error-prone, and easy to reuse on a different system by changing only RNA_HOME. The reference variables all build on RNA_REF_INDEX. The HISAT2 index prefix (chr22), the genome sequence (chr22.fa), and the annotation (chr22.gtf) share the same base name. To keep the exercise fast, we only use human chromosome 22 rather than the whole genome. Note that these variables have been copied to the .bashrc file and you need to do that when you work on your own system after the workshop. Another option is to run this block again when you open a new terminal or reconnect. # Top-level working directory for this module export RNA_HOME=~/workspace/Module6 # One directory per analysis stage export RNA_DATA_DIR=$RNA_HOME/data # raw FASTQ files export RNA_DATA_TRIM_DIR=$RNA_HOME/trimmed # adapter/quality-trimmed FASTQ files export RNA_ALIGN_DIR=$RNA_HOME/alignment # SAM/BAM alignment files export RNA_EXP_DIR=$RNA_HOME/expression # gene count tables # Reference files (chromosome 22 only) export RNA_REFS_DIR=$RNA_HOME/refs export RNA_REF_INDEX=$RNA_REFS_DIR/chr22 # prefix for the HISAT2 index files export RNA_REF_FASTA=$RNA_REF_INDEX.fa # genome sequence (FASTA) export RNA_REF_GTF=$RNA_REF_INDEX.gtf # gene annotation (GTF) To view the environment variables you can try env and for checking this module variables env | grep RNA All the tools needed are installed for you in the workshop instance environment. Follow this page from the Griffith’s lab for complete instructions for RNAseq Tool Installation 2. Explore data in your workspace The course data is stored in a shared, read-only location, so we copy it into our own workspace before working with it. The data is in FASTQ format. Each sequencing read occupies four lines: a header line starting with @ (the read name) the nucleotide sequence a + separator line a quality string with one Phred quality score per base, encoded as an ASCII character The files are gzip-compressed (.fastq.gz) to save space. Most bioinformatics tools read compressed files directly. Before any analysis, we run FastQC on each file. FastQC produces an HTML report with plots of per-base quality, GC content, sequence duplication, overrepresented sequences, and adapter content. These reports help us decide whether the reads need trimming, and they reveal problems with the library or the sequencing run. mkdir -p $RNA_HOME cp -r ~/CourseData/Module6/data $RNA_HOME # check the data cd $RNA_DATA_DIR ls # folder to collect all QC reports mkdir qc fastqc --outdir qc *.fastq.gz How many samples and replicates are there in the dataset? What is the sequencing depth of each sample? (Find the number of lines in each file and compare to QC report) What is r1 and r2 in the file names indicating? Show Answer Hints samples.txt describes the experimental design: which sample belongs to which condition and replicate. Biological replicates are needed to estimate variability when testing for differential expression later. Each read takes four lines in a FASTQ file, so dividing the line count by 4 gives the number of reads. Because the files are compressed, decompress them while counting (zcat file.fastq.gz | wc -l). Running wc -l directly on a .gz file counts lines in the compressed binary data, which is meaningless. The data is paired-end. Each DNA fragment was sequenced from both ends. Read 1 and read 2 of a pair come from the same fragment and appear in the same order in the two files. Tools must always receive both files of a pair together. cd $RNA_DATA_DIR # experimental design cat samples.txt # number of lines per file and divide by 4 for number of reads zcat MCF7_rep1_r1.fastq.gz | wc -l zcat MCF7_rep2_r1.fastq.gz | wc -l zcat MCF7_rep3_r1.fastq.gz | wc -l 3. Trimming and QC Raw reads often contain sequencing adapter sequences. Adapters appear when the cDNA fragment is shorter than the read length. Reads also tend to lose quality toward their 3′ end. Both problems can reduce alignment rates or cause misalignments. fastp scans the reads and does several things in one pass: - detects and removes adapters automatically - trims low-quality bases - discards reads that become too short - writes its own HTML/JSON QC report For paired-end data, fastp processes R1 and R2 together so that the pairs stay synchronized. If one read of a pair is discarded, its mate is handled accordingly. With many samples, opening one FastQC or fastp report per file becomes tedious. MultiQC searches a directory for reports from supported tools, including FastQC and fastp, and combines them into a single interactive report. This makes it easy to compare samples side by side and spot outliers. After running this step for all samples try MultiQC that summarizes all QC output files. mkdir -p $RNA_DATA_TRIM_DIR # example for one sample; repeat (or loop) for every sample fastp \ -i AR1_MCF7_rep1_r1.fastq.gz -I AR1_MCF7_rep1_r2.fastq.gz \ -o $RNA_DATA_TRIM_DIR/AR1_MCF7_rep1_r1.fastq.gz \ -O $RNA_DATA_TRIM_DIR/AR1_MCF7_rep1_r2.fastq.gz \ --detect_adapter_for_pe \ -h qc/AR1_MCF7_rep1_fastp.html \ -j qc/AR1_MCF7_rep1_fastp.json Practice Write the fastp trimming scripts for the other replicates Summarize all samples QC with MultiQC and view the output in your browser. # aggregate all reports found in qc/ into one summary report multiqc qc -o qc/multiqc_report 4. Prepare the reference genome for alignment Searching every read against the raw genome sequence would be far too slow. Aligners therefore first build an index, a compressed data structure that allows sequences to be looked up very quickly. HISAT2 uses a hierarchical index based on the Burrows–Wheeler transform / FM-index. This only needs to be done once per reference genome. hisat2_extract_splice_sites.py reads the GTF annotation and writes the coordinates of known exon–exon junctions. Because RNA-seq reads come from spliced mRNA, a single read can span an intron. Known junctions help HISAT2 align these split reads correctly. The file can be passed to hisat2 with --known-splicesite-infile. It can also be passed to hisat2-build with -p parallel process - provide number of cores, --ss, together with --exon from hisat2_extract_exons.py, to build a splice-aware index. hisat2-build creates the index from the FASTA file. It writes several files named chr22.1.ht2, chr22.2.ht2, and so on. The second argument (chr22) is the prefix that we later pass to hisat2 -x. samtools faidx creates a .fai index of the FASTA file. This allows tools such as samtools and IGV to retrieve any region of the genome quickly. mkdir $RNA_REFS_DIR cd $RNA_REFS_DIR # the required reference files .fa and .gtf cp ~/CourseData/Module6/refs/chr22.fa $RNA_REFS_DIR cp ~/CourseData/Module6/refs/chr22.gtf $RNA_REFS_DIR # extract known splice sites and exons from the annotation .gtf hisat2_extract_splice_sites.py chr22.gtf > chr22.splicesites.txt hisat2_extract_exons.py chr22.gtf > chr22.exons.txt # build the HISAT2 index (output files: chr22.*.ht2) hisat2-build -p 2 --ss $RNA_REF_INDEX.splicesites.txt --exon $RNA_REF_INDEX.exons.txt $RNA_REF_FASTA $RNA_REF_INDEX # FASTA index for fast random access to the sequence (creates chr22.fa.fai) samtools faidx chr22.fa 5. Alignment with HISAT2 HISAT2 is a splice-aware aligner. It maps each read pair to its location in the genome and allows a read to be split across an intron. The options used here: -x sets the index prefix. -1 and -2 give the paired read files (R1 and R2). -S names the output SAM file. --summary-file saves the alignment statistics: total reads, the percentage aligned uniquely, the percentage aligned to multiple locations, and the overall alignment rate. --rg-id and --rg SM:/LB:/PL:/PU: add read group information to the SAM header and each read. HISAT2 doesn’t need them for alignment, but some other tools often require read groups, and they help keep track of samples if you merge BAM files later. Note that --rg only works alongside --rg-id. --rg-id is a unique ID for this set of reads. The file’s base name works well. SM sample name sample group name. Just be aware if you merge aligned reads those replicates will be combined to one sample. LB library name. PL the sequencing platform ILLUMINA The overall alignment rate is one of the most important QC metrics. Here the reference is only chromosome 22, so most reads will legitimately not align. Expect a low rate. The output is in SAM format, a plain-text file with one line per alignment. SAM files are large and slow to process, so we convert them with samtools sort. This produces a BAM file, the compressed binary equivalent, and sorts the alignments by genomic coordinate. samtools index then creates a .bai index. This lets programs such as IGV and htseq-count jump directly to a genomic region without reading the whole file. Once the BAM file is created, you can delete the SAM file to save space. If you trimmed your reads in the previous step, you can align the trimmed files from $RNA_DATA_TRIM_DIR instead of the raw files. mkdir $RNA_ALIGN_DIR cd $RNA_ALIGN_DIR # align one paired-end sample to chr22 hisat2 -x $RNA_REF_INDEX \ --dta --rna-strandness RF \ -1 $RNA_DATA_DIR/AR1_MCF7_rep1_r1.fastq.gz \ -2 $RNA_DATA_DIR/AR1_MCF7_rep1_r2.fastq.gz \ -S AR1_MCF7_rep1.sam \ --summary-file AR1_MCF7_rep1_summary.txt \ --rg-id=AR1_MCF7_rep1 \ --rg SM:AR1_MCF7 \ --rg LB:AR1_MCF7_rep1 \ --rg PL:ILLUMINA # convert SAM to compressed BAM, sorted by genomic position samtools sort -o AR1_MCF7_rep1.bam AR1_MCF7_rep1.sam # index the BAM file (creates AR1_MCF7_rep1.bam.bai) samtools index AR1_MCF7_rep1.bam Practice Write the scripts for the rest of samples Explore the summary.txt output file Try FastQC on the aligned reads. FastQC accepts BAM files as input (fastqc AR1_MCF7_rep1.bam). Compare the report with the one from the raw reads. samtools flagstat AR1_MCF7_rep1.bam also gives a quick summary of mapped and properly paired reads. Merge .bam files for each group of samples to make it easier for visualization. In this step, the unique rg-id that we set for alignment becomes important to distinguish samples. # merge AR1_MCF7 bam files java -Xmx2g -jar /usr/local/picard.jar MergeSamFiles -OUTPUT AR1_MCF7.bam -INPUT AR1_MCF7_rep1.bam -INPUT AR1_MCF7_rep2.bam -INPUT AR1_MCF7_rep3.bam # merge MCF7 bam files java -Xmx2g -jar /usr/local/picard.jar MergeSamFiles -OUTPUT MCF7.bam -INPUT MCF7_rep1.bam -INPUT MCF7_rep2.bam -INPUT MCF7_rep3.bam # how many bam files do you have? ls -l *bam | wc -l Download the BAM file together with its .bai index, and try visualizing them in IGV. Remember that this data covers only chromosome 22 of the genome, so load the human reference (hg38) in IGV and navigate to chr22. Look for reads piling up on exons and for split reads spanning introns, which IGV draws as thin connecting lines. 6. Gene count estimation To measure gene expression, we count how many reads (here, read pairs) overlap the exons of each gene. The resulting table of raw counts is the input for differential expression tools such as edgeR or DESeq2. These tools expect raw, unnormalized counts. htseq-count compares each alignment with the gene annotation in the GTF file. The options used here: --format bam --order pos: the input is a BAM file sorted by position, as produced by samtools sort. For paired-end data, htseq-count needs to know the sort order to find the two mates of each pair. --mode intersection-strict: a read is counted for a gene only if the entire read falls within that gene’s exons. Reads that partly overlap introns or intergenic regions are not counted. Reads compatible with more than one gene are reported as __ambiguous rather than assigned. --stranded reverse: the library was prepared with a stranded protocol (e.g. dUTP/TruSeq Stranded), in which read 1 maps to the strand opposite the gene. Setting strandedness correctly is essential. A wrong setting can make most counts disappear or assign reads to the wrong overlapping gene. Use yes for forward-stranded libraries and no for unstranded ones. --minaqual 1: skip alignments with mapping quality below 1. This removes reads that align equally well to several locations and therefore cannot be confidently assigned. --type exon --idattr gene_id: count over exon features in the GTF, and group exons by their gene_id so that counts are reported per gene. --additional-attr gene_name: add the gene symbol as an extra column next to the gene ID, for readability. The output has one line per gene with its read count. It ends with summary lines (__no_feature, __ambiguous, __too_low_aQual, __not_aligned, __alignment_not_unique) that show how many reads were not assigned to any gene, and why. Check these lines: a very large __no_feature count often means the strandedness setting is wrong. mkdir $RNA_EXP_DIR cd $RNA_EXP_DIR htseq-count --format bam --order pos --mode intersection-strict \ --stranded reverse --minaqual 1 --type exon \ --idattr gene_id --additional-attr gene_name \ $RNA_ALIGN_DIR/AR1_MCF7_rep1.bam $RNA_REF_GTF > AR1_MCF7_rep1_genes.chr22.tsv # inspect the result head AR1_MCF7_rep1_genes.chr22.tsv tail -n 5 AR1_MCF7_rep1_genes.chr22.tsv # summary 7. Differential Expression Analysis In this section, we start from a protein-coding-only HTSeq count matrix. gene-level read counts for 6 RNA-seq samples that have already been restricted to protein-coding genes. This data contains the complete genome except non-coding RNAs, pseudogenes, etc. that were removed in an earlier filtering step. We compare MCF7 breast cancer cells across two conditions with three replicates each. the standard edgeR workflow consists of these steps: Load the count matrix and build sample metadata Filter out low-count genes Normalize library sizes (TMM) Explore the data with QC plots Estimate dispersion and fit a model Test a contrast of interest and visualize the results: AR1_MCF7 (Abemaciclib-resistant, dose 1) vs MCF7 (control) At the end of the workshop, you can use the practice expression data with two more groups (AR_MCF7 and PR_MCF7) to repeat the analysis yourself and test PR_MCF7 (Palbociclib-resistant) vs AR_MCF7 as an exercise. Transfer the expression data to your workspace, and you can move to Rstudio for the rest of this module. cd $RNA_EXP_DIR # copy the complete expression dataset and sample metadata cp ~/CourseData/Module6/expression/expression_data.txt ./ cp ~/CourseData/Module6/expression/sample_metadata.txt ./ Load packages and data Load the necessary packages, they are installed and ready to use. On your own environment you might need to install them for the first time. library(edgeR) library(ggplot2) library(ggrepel) library(DT) # work in your workspace directory setwd("~/workspace/Module6/expression/") count_file <- "expression_data.txt" metadata_file <- "sample_metadata.txt" counts <- read.delim(count_file, row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE) metadata <- read.delim(metadata_file, stringsAsFactors = FALSE) metadata$group <- factor(metadata$group) count_mat <- as.matrix(counts) dim(count_mat) head(count_mat) DT::datatable(metadata, rownames = FALSE, options = list(dom = "t")) Make a DGEList object edgeR stores counts, sample info, and (later) normalization factors and dispersions together in a single DGEList object. dge <- DGEList(counts = count_mat, group = metadata$group) dge$samples QC: sequencing depth per sample Large differences in library size are expected and are exactly what normalization corrects for – but it’s worth checking there isn’t a sample with a dramatically low read count, which could indicate a failed library. libsize_df <- data.frame(sample = factor(colnames(dge), levels = colnames(dge)), lib_size = dge$samples$lib.size / 1e6, group = metadata$group) ggplot(libsize_df, aes(x = sample, y = lib_size, fill = group)) + geom_col() + labs(title = "Sequencing depth per sample", x = NULL, y = "Library size (millions)", fill = "Group") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), plot.margin = margin(5.5, 5.5, 11, 11)) Filter out low-count genes Genes with very few reads across all samples carry little statistical power and mostly add noise (and multiple-testing burden) to the analysis. edgeR’s filterByExpr() keeps genes with enough counts to be reliably tested in at least one group. keep <- filterByExpr(dge, group = metadata$group) cat(sprintf("Keeping %d of %d genes\n", sum(keep), length(keep))) The density plot below compares log-CPM distributions before and after filtering – the discarded genes are the peak of near-zero-count genes on the far left. logcpm_before <- edgeR::cpm(dge, log = TRUE) logcpm_kept <- logcpm_before[keep, , drop = FALSE] density_df <- rbind( data.frame(logcpm = as.vector(logcpm_before), sample = rep(colnames(dge), each = nrow(logcpm_before)), set = "before filtering"), data.frame(logcpm = as.vector(logcpm_kept), sample = rep(colnames(dge), each = nrow(logcpm_kept)), set = "after filtering") ) ggplot(density_df, aes(x = logcpm, group = interaction(sample, set), color = set)) + geom_density() + scale_color_manual(values = c("before filtering" = "grey70", "after filtering" = "steelblue")) + labs(title = "log-CPM density before/after filtering", x = "log-CPM", y = "Density", color = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) Apply the gene filter to the data dge <- dge[keep, , keep.lib.sizes = FALSE] Normalize with TMM Trimmed Mean of M-values (TMM) normalization corrects for differences in RNA composition between samples (not just sequencing depth), which keeps highly-expressed genes in one sample from skewing the comparison. dge <- calcNormFactors(dge, method = "TMM") dge$samples QC: MDS plot A multidimensional scaling (MDS) plot is edgeR’s version of PCA – samples that are more similar in expression sit closer together. We expect replicates to cluster and the two groups to separate. mds <- plotMDS(dge, plot = FALSE) var_pct <- round(100 * mds$var.explained[mds$dim.plot]) mds_df <- data.frame(dim1 = mds$x, dim2 = mds$y, sample = colnames(dge), group = metadata$group) ggplot(mds_df, aes(x = dim1, y = dim2, color = group)) + geom_point(size = 3) + ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = sample), size = 3, color = "grey30", show.legend = FALSE, max.overlaps = Inf, box.padding = 0.4, segment.color = "grey60") + labs(title = "MDS plot (all samples)", x = sprintf("Leading logFC dim %d (%d%%)", mds$dim.plot[1], var_pct[1]), y = sprintf("Leading logFC dim %d (%d%%)", mds$dim.plot[2], var_pct[2]), color = "Group") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "right") Design matrix and dispersion estimation We build one design matrix for the two groups and estimate dispersion using all 6 samples together, which gives a more stable estimate than fitting each sample individually. design <- model.matrix(~0 + group, data = metadata) colnames(design) <- levels(metadata$group) design dge <- estimateDisp(dge, design, robust = TRUE) cat(sprintf("Common dispersion: %.4f (BCV = %.3f)\n", dge$common.dispersion, sqrt(dge$common.dispersion))) The biological coefficient of variation (BCV) plot shows how variance (dispersion) changes with expression level – lowly-expressed genes are typically noisier (higher BCV). plotBCV(dge, main = "Biological coefficient of variation") Fit the model and define contrasts We use a quasi-likelihood (QL) F-test (glmQLFit/glmQLFTest), which is recommended by edgeR for bulk RNA-seq as it accounts for uncertainty in the dispersion estimate and gives more robust error control than the classic likelihood-ratio test. fit <- glmQLFit(dge, design, robust = TRUE) A contrast is defined as pos - neg, so a positive logFC means higher expression in pos, and a negative logFC means higher expression in neg. We keep track of that mapping so the volcano plot can label the axis accordingly. contrasts <- makeContrasts( AR1_vs_MCF7 = AR1_MCF7 - MCF7, levels = design ) contrast_groups <- list( AR1_vs_MCF7 = c(pos = "AR1_MCF7", neg = "MCF7") ) Visualization Helper functions for visualization The same steps can be reused for any contrast (you can run a different one yourself on the practice dataset at the end), we define one function that runs the test, tables, and plots for a given contrast, and one helper that picks which genes to label on the volcano plot. Genes are ranked by a blend of significance (FDR) and effect size (|log2FC|), so the labeled genes are both strongly and significantly changed rather than just the single most extreme metric; up to 15 genes are labeled on each side (Up / Down). top_labels <- function(df, n = 15) { if (nrow(df) == 0) return(character(0)) combined_rank <- rank(df$FDR, ties.method = "average") + rank(-abs(df$logFC), ties.method = "average") df$gene[order(combined_rank)][seq_len(min(n, nrow(df)))] } run_contrast <- function(contrast_name) { qlf <- glmQLFTest(fit, contrast = contrasts[, contrast_name]) ## adjust.method = "BH" (Benjamini-Hochberg) controls the false discovery ## rate across all genes tested; it is edgeR's default, spelled out here ## since the FDR column drives both the significance calls and the ## volcano plot's y-axis. tt <- topTags(qlf, n = Inf, sort.by = "PValue", adjust.method = "BH")$table tt$gene <- rownames(tt) tt <- tt[, c("gene", setdiff(colnames(tt), "gene"))] fdr_cutoff <- 0.05 fc_cutoff <- 1 pos_group <- contrast_groups[[contrast_name]][["pos"]] neg_group <- contrast_groups[[contrast_name]][["neg"]] tt$negLog10FDR <- -log10(pmax(tt$FDR, 1e-300)) tt$status <- "Not sig." tt$status[tt$FDR < fdr_cutoff & tt$logFC >= fc_cutoff] <- "Up" tt$status[tt$FDR < fdr_cutoff & tt$logFC <= -fc_cutoff] <- "Down" tt$status <- factor(tt$status, levels = c("Down", "Not sig.", "Up")) list(qlf = qlf, table = tt, pos = pos_group, neg = neg_group, fdr_cutoff = fdr_cutoff, fc_cutoff = fc_cutoff) } plot_ma <- function(result, contrast_name) { plotMD(result$qlf, main = sprintf("MA plot: %s", contrast_name)) abline(h = 0, col = "grey40") } plot_volcano <- function(result, contrast_name) { tt <- result$table up_labels <- top_labels(tt[tt$status == "Up", ], n = 15) down_labels <- top_labels(tt[tt$status == "Down", ], n = 15) tt$label <- ifelse(tt$gene %in% c(up_labels, down_labels), tt$gene, NA) n_up <- sum(tt$status == "Up") n_down <- sum(tt$status == "Down") x_range <- range(tt$logFC, na.rm = TRUE) y_min <- min(tt$negLog10FDR, na.rm = TRUE) ggplot(tt, aes(x = logFC, y = negLog10FDR, color = status)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 1.4) + geom_vline(xintercept = c(-result$fc_cutoff, result$fc_cutoff), linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") + geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(result$fdr_cutoff), linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") + ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = label), color = "black", size = 3, max.overlaps = Inf, min.segment.length = 0, box.padding = 0.4, segment.color = "grey40", na.rm = TRUE, show.legend = FALSE) + scale_color_manual(values = c("Down" = "#0072B2", "Not sig." = "grey80", "Up" = "#D55E00"), drop = FALSE) + annotate("text", x = x_range[1], y = y_min, label = paste("<- higher in", result$neg), hjust = 0, vjust = 1.5, size = 3, color = "grey40", fontface = "italic") + annotate("text", x = x_range[2], y = y_min, label = paste("higher in", result$pos, "->"), hjust = 1, vjust = 1.5, size = 3, color = "grey40", fontface = "italic") + labs(title = sprintf("Volcano plot: %s", contrast_name), subtitle = sprintf("%d up / %d down (BH FDR < %.2f, |log2FC| >= %g); labeled: up to 15 per side (FDR + |FC|)", n_up, n_down, result$fdr_cutoff, result$fc_cutoff), x = sprintf("log2 fold-change (%s vs %s)", result$pos, result$neg), y = "-log10(FDR, BH-adjusted)", color = NULL) + coord_cartesian(clip = "off") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"), plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey30", size = 9), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), legend.position = "top", plot.margin = margin(5.5, 5.5, 11, 5.5)) } AR1_MCF7 vs MCF7 In the following steps we will use the helper functions to run the differential analysis and visualize results. Compare Abemaciclib resistant MCF7 cells to the parental MCF7 samples. res_ar1 <- run_contrast("AR1_vs_MCF7") # write results table write.table(res_ar1$qlf, "AR1_vs_MCF7.txt", sep = '\t') # View summary summary(decideTests(res_ar1$qlf)) Create mean-difference plot (aka MA plot) which shows log fold-changes on the y-axis against average expression on the x-axis, and colour highlights differentially expressed genes in a fitted model. plot_ma(res_ar1, "AR1_vs_MCF7") Generate the volcano plot, colour and label the differentially expressed genes. plot_volcano(res_ar1, "AR1_vs_MCF7") Explore the complete table of DE results DT::datatable(res_ar1$table[, c("gene", "logFC", "logCPM", "PValue", "FDR")], rownames = FALSE, filter = "top", options = list(pageLength = 10)) |> DT::formatSignif(columns = c("logFC", "logCPM", "PValue", "FDR"), digits = 3) For practice, you can copy/download the practice data from ~/CourseData/Module6/practice/expression/practice_expression_data.txt and ~/CourseData/Module6/practice/expression/practice_sample_metadata.txt and make the changes in this script for differential expression analysis between the two drug resistant cell groups, Abemaciclib-resistant (AR_MCF7) vs. Palbociclib-resistant (PR_MCF7) Show Hints Hints: add the respective file paths to the above R script pay attention to the new design matrix generated with the sample metadata make changes to the contrasts and contrast_groups using the sample names from design helper functions remain the same run the final steps with the new contrasts for PR vs AR sample groups
