Module 7 | From Gene Alteration to Gene Effect Lecture Lab

Module 7 | From Gene Alteration to Gene Effect Lecture Lab Part 1. Introduction Author: Aqsa Alam 1.1: Description of the Lab In previous modules, you learned how to identify somatic variants. But identifying a variant is only the first step. What does that variant actually mean? A change in a DNA sequence does not automatically mean that a gene is dysfunctional or that the change contributes to cancer. To investigate its potential effect, we need to understand where the variant occurs, predict its molecular consequence, and examine what is already known about the affected gene and its variant. In this lab, you will explore somatic variants from two pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) cases using bcftools and awk, and annotate those variants using SnpEff. You will explore the resulting annotations and HTML summary reports to investigate the types of variants present and their predicted effects on genes and transcripts. You will then examine selected variants in the context of existing databases and scientific evidence. To explore differences in annotation algorithms, you will also use Ensembl Variant Effect Predictor (VEP) to investigate a variant of your choice. Throughout the lab, keep one thing in mind: a predicted consequence is not the same thing as a demonstrated functional effect, and does not automatically establish that the variant contributes to cancer. Your goal is to use the available evidence to develop an informed hypothesis of what the variants might mean. 1.2: Our data The data we will be using in this lab has been downloaded from the International Cancer Genome Consortium (ICGC) ARGO Data Platform, from a study of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) called PACA-CA (Pancreatic Cancer Harmonized ‘Omics’ analysis for Personalized Treatment).The study is also described here. The dataset consists of two tumour samples, each from a different patient, which was analyzed using a matched normal (in which DNA from a patient’s tumour is analyzed alongside DNA from a normal blood sample from the same patient). This comparison helps distinguish variants in the tumour from variants in the patient’s healthy cells. DATA SOURCES 2. Patient 1: Single-Nucleotide Variants (SNVs) PACA-CA.DO49419.SA520262.wgs.20201012.gatk-mutect2.somatic.snv.open-filter.vcf.gz 1. Patient 2: Insertions and Deletions (InDels) PACA-CA.DO35350.SA520304.wgs.20201011.gatk-mutect2.somatic.indel.open-filter.vcf.gz Both datasets have the following features: Assay: Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) Instrument: Illumina Genome build: GRCh38 Variant caller: GATK Mutect2 File processing: bcftools view Sample type: Primary tumour, with matched normal sequencing used for somatic variant calling Access: Open-access, filtered VCF The two cases contain different sets of variants: Case Variant set Genes of interest Patient 1 Single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) KRAS, BRCA2 Patient 2 Insertions and deletions (InDels) SMAD4, TP53 Note: These are two separate patients, not one combined tumour profile. The raw VCF data has been significantly filtered as per ICGC ARGO’s Open Access Variant Filtering workflow. Open access regions are also described in detail here. This is to prevent accidental disclosure of germline variants which might identify a patient and compromise their privacy. This gives us the ability to explore real cancer data without the need for special permissions, at the expense of some data loss. Before running any commands, consider: 1. What information can we get from a list of genomic variants? 2. If we know that a variant occurs in a cancer-associated gene, do we know what the variant does? 1.3: Our tools We will use three command-line tools, one web-based tool, and explore some databases. bcftools bcftools is a collection of tools for working with VCF and BCF files. In this lab, we will use it to inspect variant calls, count records, and examine fields. To see the manual for bcftools, try one of the following commands: $ bcftools --help $ man bcftools SnpEff SnpEff annotates genetic variants by comparing their genomic positions and alleles with existing gene and transcript annotations. It predicts consequences such as: missense variant: a coding change that alters an amino acid synonymous variant: a coding change that does not alter an amino acid stop_gained or nonsense variant: a change that introduces a premature stop codon frameshift_variant: an insertion or deletion that shifts the coding reading frame intron_variant: a variant located within an intron SnpEff also annotates variants by impact level: HIGH impact: the variant is assumed to have disruptive impact in the protein and probably causes protein truncation, loss of function, or nonsense-mediated decay MODERATE impact: a non-disruptive variant that might change protein effectiveness LOW impact: assumed to be mostly harmless or unlikely to change protein behaviour MODIFIER impact: usually non-coding variants or variants affecting non-coding genes, where predictions are difficult or there is no evidence of impact The documentation is the most thorough source of explanations for SnpEff outputs. You may find this useful to consult during the lab: SnpEff Documentation. To see the manual for SnpEff, try the following command: $ java -jar /usr/local/snpEff/snpEff.jar --help Important consideration: SnpEff predicts molecular consequences. It does not determine that a variant changes protein function, causes cancer, or predicts response to treatment. awk awk is a command-line tool for processing and analyzing structured text. It reads input line by line, splits each line into fields (by default, separated by whitespace), and lets you select, extract, or manipulate specific fields. It is extremely useful for pattern-matching and extracting particular lines from a VCF-file, such as looking for lines that contain particular genes of interest. To see the manual for awk, try one of the following commands: $ awk --help $ man awk Ensembl Variant Effect Predictor (VEP) (From the homepage:) Ensembl VEP predicts the effect of your variants (SNPs, insertions, deletions, CNVs or structural variants) on gene transcripts and protein sequence, as well as regulatory regions. It reports reference data including gene and variant phenotype associations and population allele frequencies to facilitate variant prioritisation and interpretation. You can access Ensembl VEP here: Ensembl VEP Homepage The web browser version is here: Ensembl VEP Web Browser Version (note: the browser version is very slow and often times out. If you get a time out error, just refresh and try again). Variant Databases Lastly, we will explore several databases that collect and organize existing evidence about genetic variants. These resources can help us investigate whether a variant has been previously reported, what is known about its clinical significance, and whether it may be relevant to cancer diagnosis or treatment. CIViC: A community-curated database of evidence linking cancer variants to clinical significance, including potential implications for diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment. OncoKB: A precision oncology knowledge base that summarizes the biological and clinical significance of cancer alterations, including evidence for their relevance to specific therapies. ClinVar: A public database of submitted interpretations of genetic variants and their relationships to health conditions. Entries may differ in their evidence, classification, and relevance to the cancer context being investigated. Important consideration: Databases are often built by public submission or curated from published literature. A database entry does not automatically establish that a variant drives cancer or is clinically actionable. Similarly, a variant missing from a database does not automatically imply that the variant is not involved in cancer or is not clinically actionable. The variant may simply not have been reported or evaluated yet. The absence of evidence is not evidence of absence! Part 2: Inspect the data 2.1. Copy the files Navigate to your workspace directory and create a subdirectory for your work (call it whatever you want; here, I’m calling it module7): $ cd workspace/ $ mkdir module7 $ cd module7 Copy the VCF files to your workspace. We will simplify the file names for the rest of the workshop.List the files: $ cp ../CourseData/Module7/PACA-CA.DO49419.SA520262.wgs.20201012.gatk-mutect2.somatic.snv.open-filter.vcf.gz patient1_snvs.vcf.gz $ cp ../CourseData/Module7/PACA-CA.DO35350.SA520304.wgs.20201011.gatk-mutect2.somatic.indel.open-filter.vcf.gz patient2_indels.vcf.gz $ ls Questions: Which files have been provided?? Which one contains SNVs? Which ones contains indels? What file extension do you see? What might it indicate? 2.2. Examine the VCF header VCF stands for Variant Call Format. It is a standard format used in bioinformatics for representing genetic variants. First, display the header of Patient 1’s VCF: $ bcftools view -h patient1_snvs.vcf.gz | less Do the same for patient 2. Examine the header. A VCF contains two main components: Header lines, beginning with #, that describe the file, reference genome, samples, and fields. Variant records, which describe individual variants The header ends with a column-name line beginning with #CHROM. Questions: What do the following FORMAT fields represent: DP, AD, AF? What do the following FILTER fields represent: PASS, map_qual, germline? What version of Mutect was used to process the results? What does PASS indicate? 2.3. Understand the VCF columns Each variant record describes a difference between the reference genome and an observed alternate allele. Column Meaning CHROM Chromosome or contig containing the variant POS Genomic position of the variant ID Variant identifier, if available REF Reference allele ALT Alternate allele QUAL Variant-call quality score FILTER Whether the record passed the applied filters INFO Additional information about the variant FORMAT Description of sample-level fields Sample column(s) Genotype and other sample-level information For example, a simplified record might look like this: chr1 1778559 . G A . PASS DP=29 GT:AD 0|1:8,3 0|0:18,0 Here, the reference allele is G, while the alternate allele is A. The total sequencing depth (DP) is 29 reads. The AD field indicates the number of reads supporting each allele, in reference–alternate order. The first sample has 8 reads supporting the reference allele and 3 supporting the alternate allele, while the second sample has 18 reads supporting the reference allele and 0 supporting the alternate allele. The GT field indicates the genotype of each sample: 0|1 for the first sample and 0|0 for the second sample. Questions Which column tells you where a variant occurs? Which columns tell you what sequence was observed and what sequence it differs from? Does a PASS record necessarily represent a cancer-driving mutation? Does the presence of an alternate allele (an allele different from the reference sequence) mean that the variant is somatic (i.e, acquired in the tumour rather than inherited)? 2.4. Look at the first few variant records Display the first five variant records from Patient 1: $ bcftools view -H patient1_snvs.vcf.gz | head -n 5 The -H option excludes the header, allowing you to see only variant records. The head command limits the output to the first five lines. Repeat for Patient 2: $ bcftools view -H patient2_indels.vcf.gz | head -n 5 Questions What type of information can you read directly from these records? What do you notice about the difference between the ALT fields in the patient with the SNV data vs. the patient with the indel data? Can you identify a gene from these columns alone? Can you determine the effect of a variant on a protein from the REF and ALT fields alone? Why might two variants with different genomic positions have very different biological consequences? Part 3. Summarize the variant calls with bcftools Before annotating the variants, we should understand the contents of our input files. 3.1. Count the variant records Count the number of variant records in Patient 1’s VCF: $ bcftools view -H patient1_snvs.vcf.gz | wc -l Repeat for Patient 2: $ bcftools view -H patient2_indels.vcf.gz | wc -l The wc -l command counts the number of lines. Here, each line represents a variant record. Questions Which file contains more variant records? Does having more called variants mean that a tumour is more aggressive? Why should we avoid comparing these counts without knowing how the samples and variant sets were generated? 3.2. Generate a summary with bcftools stats Run the following command for Patient 1: $ bcftools stats patient1_snvs.vcf.gz > patient1_stats.txt Then inspect the summary: $ less patient1_stats.txt Press q to exit less. Repeat for Patient 2: $ bcftools stats patient2_indels.vcf.gz > patient2_stats.txt The output includes summary statistics about the VCF records. Depending on the input, these can include the number of records, SNPs, insertions, deletions, transitions, transversions, and other metrics. You can also find the relevant statistics directly with: $ grep '^SN' patient1_stats.txt $ grep '^SN' patient2_stats.txt Questions How many records does the summary report? How many samples does the summary report? Why are there this many number of samples? Finish examining the stats, then exit with q. Part 4. Annotate variants with SnpEff 4.1. What are we adding to the VCF? So far, our VCF tells us where the variants are and which alternate alleles were called. However, the records may not directly tell us whether a variant lies within a coding exon, changes an amino acid, introduces a stop codon, or affects a splice site. SnpEff uses an existing genome annotation database to predict these consequences. Conceptually, the process is: Variant coordinates and alleles + reference genome and gene annotations = predicted molecular consequences SnpEff does not experimentally test each protein. Instead, it applies standardized computational rules to available sequence and annotation information to generate consistent, reproducible predictions of variant effects. 4.2: Exploring Available SnpEff Databases Before annotating variants, SnpEff needs a database containing reference genome and gene annotation information. The database determines which genes and transcripts SnpEff uses to predict the consequences of each variant. SnpEff provides a command to list available genome databases. Run: $ java -jar /usr/local/snpEff/snpEff.jar databases | less You can also search the output for human genome databases associated with GRCh38: $ java -jar /usr/local/snpEff/snpEff.jar databases | grep 'GRCh38' The output lists database identifiers and information about their availability. Depending on the SnpEff installation, it may include databases that are configured but not yet downloaded. While we have already installed the database we need, GRCh38.p14, you can install any database using the download command. Questions Why is it important to use a database compatible with the reference genome used to call the variants? The reference genome that was used to generate the VCFs for this lab was GRCh38, so we will be using GRCh38.p14 (the .p14 bit refers to a patch release or fix). 4.3. Annotattion Run SnpEff on Patient 1’s SNV VCF: $ java -jar /usr/local/snpEff/snpEff.jar -v -stats patient1_snpeff_summary.html GRCh38.p14 patient1_snvs.vcf.gz > patient1_snvs_annotated.vcf This command has several components: java -jar /usr/local/snpEff/snpEff.jar: runs SnpEff. -v: enables verbose output. -stats patient1_snpeff_summary.html: requests an HTML summary report. GRCh38.p14: specifies the genome annotation database. patient1_snvs.vcf.gz: the input VCF. >: redirects the annotated VCF output into a new file. patient1_snvs_annotated.vcf: the output file containing the annotations. The original VCF remains unchanged. Repeat the process for Patient 2: $ java -jar /usr/local/snpEff/snpEff.jar -v -stats patient2_snpeff_summary.html GRCh38.p14 patient2_indels.vcf.gz > patient2_indels_annotated.vcf You can use the following list command to see new files at the top of the list: $ ls -lt Questions Which new files were generated? Why is it useful to preserve the original VCF rather than overwrite it? What information do you expect to find in the annotated VCF that was absent from the original file? What assumptions does this annotation process rely on? 4.4. Inspect the annotated VCF First, inspect the header of the annotated file: $ bcftools view -h patient1_snvs_annotated.vcf | less Look for an INFO field called ANN by doing the following in less: /ANN(hit enter) Inspect the line. This tells you how to read the new annotations. The ANN field contains predicted annotations associated with each variant. These can include the predicted consequence, impact category, gene, transcript, and other information. Now inspect the first five annotated variant records and look at the ANN field. $ bcftools view -H patient1_snvs_annotated.vcf | head -n 5 Questions What has changed between the original and annotated VCFs? Which original fields have been retained? Where are the annotations stored? Does adding an annotation change the underlying variant call? Why might a single variant have more than one annotation? Repeat the above steps with Patient 2. Part 5. Interpret the SnpEff HTML summary 5.1. Open the summary report Open patient1_snpeff_summary.html in your web browser. Repeat with patient2_snpeff_summary.html. These reports provide an overview of the consequences predicted across the input variant set. Explore the summary and consider what each statistic represents. The report includes information such as: Counts of variants and annotations. Predicted variant effects or consequences. Impact categories. Genes affected by variants. Distribution of consequences across different genomic regions. Questions What is the largest effect by impact: high, low, moderate, or modifier? Is this the same for Patient 2? Why is it the largest category? Can you conclude that one patient’s cancer is more aggressive from these summaries alone? Why would it be misleading to rank patients by the number of HIGH-impact annotations alone? Why might a single variant have more than one annotation? Part 6. Examine individual variant annotations The summary tells us what is present across the dataset. Now we will examine individual records to understand what SnpEff predicts for particular variants. 6.1. Extract the ANN field Use bcftools query to extract the variant coordinates, alleles, and SnpEff annotation field, so we are not distracted by other fields in the VCF when viewing annotations: $ bcftools query -f '%CHROM\t%POS\t%REF\t%ALT\t%INFO/ANN\n' patient1_snvs_annotated.vcf > patient1_annotations.tsv Inspect the output: $ head -n 5 patient1_annotations.tsv Repeat for Patient 2. The output is a tab-separated file containing the genomic location, reference allele, alternate allele, and ANN annotations. A single ANN field may contain multiple annotations, separated by commas. Within an individual annotation, fields are separated by vertical bars (|). Questions What do the first four fields of an ANN entry represent? What is the difference between a variant’s predicted consequence and its impact category? Why can a single genomic variant have multiple ANN entries? 6.2. Investigate a variant in a gene of interest Select a variant annotated in one of the genes of interest for your patient. Patient 1: investigate a variant in KRAS or BRCA2. Patient 2: investigate a variant in SMAD4 or TP53. These genes are known to be altered in PDAC. You can search the annotation file using awk: $ cat patient1_snvs_annotated.vcf | awk '/KRAS/' Use the annotated VCF and the extracted annotation table to find the relevant record. Record the following information for one of the transcripts: Question Your answer Gene Chromosome and position Reference allele (REF) Alternate allele (ALT) Coding change (c.?), if available) Protein change (p.?), if available) Predicted consequence SnpEff impact category Transcript identifier, if available (Note: for information about coding and protein change notation, see here: HGVS Nomenclature Questions What does the annotation allow you to conclude? What remains unknown? 6.3. Interpret the consequence Use the following guide to interpret common consequence terms. Consequence What it generally means missense_variant A coding change predicts a different amino acid synonymous_variant A coding change predicts the same amino acid stop_gained A change introduces a premature stop codon frameshift_variant An insertion or deletion changes the reading frame of a coding sequence splice_donor_variant A variant affects a splice donor region splice_acceptor_variant A variant affects a splice acceptor region intron_variant A variant lies within an intron 3_prime_UTR_variant A variant lies in the 3′ untranslated region upstream_gene_variant A variant lies upstream of a gene, according to the annotation These terms describe predicted molecular consequences relative to annotated genomic features and transcripts. They do not, by themselves, establish the full biological effect. Questions Which of these consequences could directly alter the amino acid sequence? Why might a synonymous variant still be biologically relevant in some circumstances? Why could an intronic or untranslated-region variant matter even if it does not change an amino acid? Does every frameshift have the same effect on a gene? Part 7. From gene function to cancer interpretation A molecular consequence is only one part of variant interpretation. To understand the potential significance of a variant, we also need to understand the gene and investigate the available evidence. 7.1. Investigate the gene Choose the gene associated with the variant you selected. You should have the coding or protein change in hand. For example, one entry is: chr1 13421103 G A A|missense_variant|MODERATE|PRAMEF20|PRAMEF20|transcript|NM_001099852.2|protein_coding|4/4|c.1273G>A|p.Val425Ile|1372/1597|1273/1428|425/475|| In this example entry, we can see the following gene, coding change, and protein change: Gene: PRAMEF20 Coding change: c.1273G>A Protein change: p.Val425Ile Search the literature for your variant (a cursory Google search is usually a good place to start. Supply the gene, coding notation, and protein change if applicable). You can use GeneCards for information about human genes. You can also use NCBI’s variation viewer to look at collated information for the variant, including in dbSNP: NCBI variation viewer. For this resource, type in the chromosome and coordinates in the search bar (ex. chr13: 32379471-32379471) and scroll down to see exact or nearby variants. Questions Why does knowing a gene’s function help us interpret a variant? What is the pathogenicity of your variant (pathogenic, benign, etc)? If a gene is a tumour suppressor, does every variant in that gene disrupt its function? What is the difference between a plausible hypothesis and a demonstrated functional effect? 7.2. Investigate variant evidence Look at the following resources: CIViC: a community-curated resource containing evidence about the clinical significance of variants in cancer. OncoKB: a precision oncology knowledge base that summarizes the biological and clinical significance of cancer alterations, including evidence for their relevance to specific therapies. ClinVar: a public database of submitted interpretations of genetic variants and their relationships to health conditions. Look up your selected variant or gene where possible. Record whether you find a matching variant, a relevant gene-level entry, or no useful record. Resource What did you find? What can you infer? CIViC OncoKB ClinVar If you cannot find the exact variant, record that result rather than substituting a different variant in the same gene without noting the distinction. Questions What kind of information does each resource provide? Does finding a variant in a cancer database prove that it drives cancer? Does a ClinVar entry automatically establish that a variant is pathogenic or benign? Why or why not? If a database has no entry for your variant, does that mean the variant has no biological or clinical significance? Why might two variants in the same gene have very different levels of evidence? What additional information might be needed before concluding that a variant contributes to the development of this patient’s cancer? Part 8. Compare SnpEff and Ensembl VEP SnpEff is not the only tool used to annotate variants. Ensembl’s Variant Effect Predictor (VEP) is another widely used tool for predicting the consequences of genetic variants. For this exercise, use the Ensembl VEP web interface: Ensembl VEP Web Interface The browser version may be slow or time out. If this happens, you may just need to try again. Select up to three variants from your annotated VCF file, i.e. the _annotated.vcf file (you can also use variants from the four known oncogenic genes provided above) Copy the chromosome, position, reference allele, and alternate allele into the VEP interface using the required input format. Below is an example. There is no need to copy the whole line; you can stop at the FILTER column. chr13 32379471 . G A . PASS Select a reference assembly that matches the input data. In our case, we will use GRCh38.p14. Run the annotation and inspect the results. You can click on the “run instant VEP for current line” button for faster results. Compare the predicted consequences with those reported by SnpEff. Record your comparison: Variant SnpEff consequence VEP consequence Same or different? Variant 1 Variant 2 Variant 3 Questions Did the tools predict the same consequence for every variant? If they differed, did they annotate the same transcript? Could differences in transcript selection, annotation releases, or prediction rules explain the discrepancy? If both tools agree, does this experimentally confirm the predicted effect? If they disagree, what would you investigate before deciding how to interpret the variant? Do not assume that one tool is automatically correct. A discrepancy is a reason to investigate the underlying annotations and assumptions. Part 9. Final interpretation Return to the variant you selected. Write a short interpretation of your favourite variant. Your response should address the following: The alteration: What is the genomic variant? The annotation: What molecular consequence did SnpEff predict? The gene: What is the normal function of the affected gene, and how is it relevant to cancer? The evidence: What did you find in the databases or literature? The hypothesis: What effect might this variant have? The uncertainty: What can you not conclude from the available information? Your interpretation should distinguish between a predicted molecular consequence, a demonstrated functional effect, a contribution to cancer, and a potential clinical implication. You are not expected to prove that your selected variant is a cancer driver. You are expected to make a reasoned interpretation of the available evidence and explain its limitations. Final questions Why is a gene’s function not enough to determine the effect of an individual variant? What additional evidence would help establish whether a variant contributes to cancer? What would you need to know before deciding whether a variant could inform treatment? Key takeaway A variant annotation is a starting point for interpretation, not the final answer. We began with a difference in DNA sequence, used genome annotations to predict its molecular consequence, investigated the affected gene and available evidence, and then formed our hypothesis.

Module 8 - Pathway Enrichment Analysis Lecture Presentation of the dataset Lab

Module 8 - Pathway Enrichment Analysis Veronique Voisin This module will cover how to use differential expression output to generate pathway enrichment results. Lecture Presentation of the dataset This module is a continuation of the transcriptomics module 6 and we will use the same dataset. This dataset contains bulk RNA-seq data of a model of breast cancer. The gene counts were deposited to the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database under accession GSE222367 and are publicly available. RNA was extracted from MCF7, a breast cancer cell line under different conditions: parental cell line and cell line samples resistant to the drugs palbociclib or abemaciclib. Biological replicates were available for each condition. RNA-seq library was prepared and sequenced using an Illumina HiSeq 2500 sequencer. Sequence reads were mapped to the human reference genome (Gencode GRCh38) using TopHat as aligner. The BAM files with mapped reads for each sample were sorted and then used as input for HTSeq 0.11.0 in order to generate read count data at the gene level. We retrieved the gene counts and performed differential expression analysis using a negative binomial generalized linear model, followed by pathway enrichment analysis. Install and load libraries ## CRAN and Bioconductor setup if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("BiocManager") ## List of CRAN packages cran_packages <- c( "tidyverse", "ggrepel" ) # List of Bioconductor packages bioc_packages <- c( "edgeR" ) # Install CRAN packages if not already installed for (pkg in cran_packages) { if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) { install.packages(pkg) } } # Install Bioconductor packages if not already installed for (pkg in bioc_packages) { if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) { BiocManager::install(pkg) } } # Load the libraries # CRAN packages library(tidyverse) ## Warning: package 'ggplot2' was built under R version 4.4.3 ## Warning: package 'purrr' was built under R version 4.4.3 ## Warning: package 'dplyr' was built under R version 4.4.3 ## ── Attaching core tidyverse packages ── tidyverse 2.0.0 ── ## ✔ dplyr 1.2.1 ✔ purrr 1.2.2 ## ✔ forcats 1.0.1 ✔ stringr 1.6.0 ## ✔ ggplot2 4.0.3 ✔ tibble 3.3.1 ## ✔ lubridate 1.9.5 ✔ tidyr 1.3.2 ## ── Conflicts ──────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ── ## ✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter() ## ✖ purrr::flatten() masks jsonlite::flatten() ## ✖ dplyr::lag() masks stats::lag() ## ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors library(ggrepel) ## Warning: package 'ggrepel' was built under R version 4.4.3 # Bioconductor packages library(edgeR) ## Loading required package: limma # create the results folder (if it does not exist yet) to save the outputs # dir.create("results", showWarnings = FALSE) # Location of the Module 8 files (data/, BYODdata/, image/): # - on the course server: ~/CourseData/Module8 # - when the book is built from the repository: Module8 data_dir <- if (dir.exists("~/CourseData/Module8")) "~/CourseData/Module8" else "Module8" Data used for this comparison For this analysis, we are going to compare the Palbo-resistant cell lines (3 biological replicates) versus the parental cell lines (3 biological replicates) Figure 2: GEO dataset generate a DGE object # 1. Find the count files files <- list.files(path = file.path(data_dir, "data"), pattern = "\\.txt\\.gz$", full.names = TRUE) # 2. Sample names from the file names (strip the extension) samples <- sub("_S.*", "", basename(files)) # 3. Read the files into a DGEList # HTSeq output has no header: column 1 = gene ID, column 2 = count. # R reads gzipped files directly, so no need to decompress. dge <- readDGE(files, columns = c(1, 2), header = FALSE, labels = samples) ## Meta tags detected: __no_feature, __ambiguous, __too_low_aQual, __not_aligned, __alignment_not_unique # 4. Remove HTSeq summary rows (__no_feature, __ambiguous, etc.) dge <- dge[!grepl("^__", rownames(dge)), , keep.lib.sizes = FALSE] # 5. (Optional) add group information dge$samples$group <- factor( c("parental", "parental", "parental", "palbo_resistant", "palbo_resistant", "palbo_resistant"), levels = c("parental", "palbo_resistant") # parental = reference ) Filter low-count genes and TMM-normalize keep <- filterByExpr(dge, group = dge$samples$group) dge <- dge[keep, , keep.lib.sizes = FALSE] dge <- calcNormFactors(dge, method = "TMM") cat("Genes retained after filtering:", nrow(dge), "\n") ## Authors: Veronique Voisin, Ruth Isserlin Presenter: Veronique Voisin Introduction During this practical lab, we will perform pathway enrichment analysis using a defined gene list. Goal of the exercise 1 For this exercise, our goal is to run pathway enrichment analysis using g:Profiler and explore the results. g:Profiler performs a gene-set enrichment analysis using a hypergeometric test (Fisher’s exact test). The Gene Ontology Biological Process, Reactome and WikiPathways sources are going to be used as pathway databases. We wil also upload our custom geneset file. g:Profiler can be used using the website at https://biit.cs.ut.ee/gprofiler/gost. However, for this practical lab, we will run it from the g:Profiler R package. We will run the query and explore the table of results and visualize the results as bar and dot plots. One of the greatest features of g:Profiler is that it is updated on a regular basis and most of the previous versions are available online ont the gprofiler archive. The gprofielr2 -g:Profiler R implementation is a wrapper for the web version. You require an internet connection to get enrichment results. Data g:Profiler requires a list of genes. For this analysis, we used genes we found to be differentially expressed in palbociclib-resistant samples compared with parental samples from the breast cancer cell line MCF7 (see chapter 1. Exercise 1 - prepare the gene lists This exercise requires the file “edgeR_resistant_vs_parental_all_genes.csv” located in the data folder. Step 1 - Install and Load libraries # List of CRAN packages cran_packages <- c( "tidyverse", "knitr", "kableExtra", "glue", "patchwork", "ggdendro", "pheatmap", "gprofiler2" ) # Install CRAN packages if not already installed for (pkg in cran_packages) { if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) { install.packages(pkg) } } # Load the libraries library(tidyverse) library(knitr) library(kableExtra) library(glue) library(patchwork) library(ggdendro) library(pheatmap) library(gprofiler2) # create the results folder (if it does not exist yet) to save the outputs # dir.create("results", showWarnings = FALSE) # Location of the Module 8 files (data/, BYODdata/, image/): # - on the course server: ~/CourseData/Module8 # - when the book is built from the repository: Module8 data_dir <- if (dir.exists("~/CourseData/Module8")) "~/CourseData/Module8" else "Module8" Step 2 - Prepare the define gene lists res = read.csv(file.path(data_dir, "data/edgeR_resistant_vs_parental_all_genes.csv")) UPgenes <- res$gene[res$logFC>0 & res$FDR <= 0.001] DOWNgenes <- res$gene[res$logFC<0 & res$FDR <= 0.001] Step 3 - Run g:Profiler The next step is to run pathway enrichment analysis using gost g:Profiler using the g:Profiler2 R package. For detailed descriptions of all the parameters that can be specified for the gost g:profiler function see the R package information - here and here. For this query we are specifying - query - the set of genes of interest, as loaded in from the gene list file (query_set). significant - set to TRUE so that g:Profiler returns only the pathways that it deems significant (adjusted p-value below its default threshold of 0.05). We will filter these results further in a next step. ordered_query - set to FALSE (because we are not taking into account the order of the list) exclude_iea - set to TRUE. We are removing the electronic inferred annotations from the GO database correction_method - set to fdr. by default g:Profiler uses g:Scs organism - set to “hsapiens” for homo sapiens. Organism names are constructed by concatenating the first letter of the name and the family name (according to gprofiler2 documentation) source - the geneset source databases to use for the analysis. We recommend using GO biological process (GO:BP), WikiPathways (WP) and Reactome (Reac) but there are additional sources you can add (GO molecular function or cellular component(GO:MF, GO:CC), KEGG, transcription factors (TF), microRNA targets (MIRNA), corum complexes (CORUM), Human protein atlas (HPA),Human phenotype ontology (HP) ) evcodes - set to TRUE so that g:Profiler also returns the genes of our list found in each pathway (column intersection, genes separated by a comma). It makes the query a little slower. run g:Profiler with the up genes query_set = UPgenes gprofiler_results_UPgenes <- gost(query = query_set , significant=TRUE, ordered_query = FALSE, exclude_iea=TRUE, correction_method = "fdr", organism = "hsapiens", source = c("REAC","WP","GO:BP"), evcodes = TRUE) observe the results #get the gprofiler results table enrichment_results <- gprofiler_results_UPgenes$result #display the names of all columns colnames(enrichment_results) ## Upload your own genesets. The most common reasons for supplying your own genesets is the ability to use up to date annotations or in-house annotations that might not be available in the public sphere yet. It can be used to test the enrichment in a particular pathway of interest that might not be in the general pathway database but that you obtained for example by extracting the data from a published paper. You need to format this pathway in a .gmt file. In this example, we will upload the Baderlab gene set file that contains multiple database sources. We filtered the gene-set prior to uploading the gene-set file to g:Profiler. The Baderlab gene set file combines different sources of databases and you can find more information at: https://baderlab.org/GeneSets ’‘’Why do we filter the geneset before running gprofiler’’’ The g:Profiler interface only allows for filtering genesets by size only after the analysis is complete. After the analysis is complete means the filtering is happening after Multiple hypothesis testing. Filtering prior to the analysis will generate more robust results because we exclude the uninformative large genesets prior to testing changing the sets that multiple hypothesis filtering will get rid of. We have 1 example of gmt files with different filtering thresholds : * genesets less of equal than 500 genes The format of the GMT file is described https://software.broadinstitute.org/cancer/software/gsea/wiki/index.php/Data_formats#GMT:Gene_Matrix_Transposed_file_format.28.2A.gmt.29 and consists of rows with the following Name Description tab delimited list of genes a part of this geneset Write out the gmt file with genenames In order to use your own genesets with g:Profiler you need to upload the the file to g:Profiler server first. The function will return an ID that you need to specify in the organism parameter of the g:Profiler gost function call. It is done by using the upload_GMT_file() function which is included in the gprofiler2 package. Note: it took about 2 minutes to run this chunck of code. dest_gmt_file_500 =file.path(data_dir, "data/Human_GOBP_AllPathways_filtered_500orLessV2.gmt") custom_gmt_max500 <- upload_GMT_file( gmtfile=dest_gmt_file_500) ## Your custom annotations ID is gp__vCna_BO6W_hJ4. ## You can use this ID as an 'organism' name in all the related enrichment tests against this custom source. ## Just use: gost(my_genes, organism = 'gp__vCna_BO6W_hJ4') UPgenes <- res$gene[res$logFC>0 & res$FDR <= 0.001] DOWNgenes <- res$gene[res$logFC<0 & res$FDR <= 0.001] gprofiler_results_custom_max500_UPgenes <- gost(query = UPgenes , significant=TRUE, ordered_query = FALSE, exclude_iea=TRUE, correction_method = "fdr", organism = custom_gmt_max500, evcodes = TRUE ) ## Detected custom GMT source request enrichment_results_UPgenes <- gprofiler_results_custom_max500_UPgenes$result enrichment_results_UPgenes$parents <- sapply( enrichment_results_UPgenes$parents, function(x) paste(x, collapse = ", ") ) gprofiler_results_custom_max500_UPgenes$result enrichment_results_UPgenes$score = -log10(as.numeric(enrichment_results_UPgenes$p_value)) enrichment <- enrichment_results_UPgenes %>% as_tibble() %>% arrange(desc(score)) %>% slice_head(n = 20) p = ggplot(enrichment, aes(reorder(term_name, score), score)) + geom_col(aes(fill = score), width=0.8) + scale_fill_gradient(low = "#C1F6F8", high = "#00BFC4")+ coord_flip() + labs(x="", y="Normalized Enrichment Score",title="Pathway enrichment analysis ") + theme_minimal() p Step 2 - Dot plot with segment enrichmentTop20 <- enrichment %>% arrange(desc(score)) %>% slice_head(n = 20) p = ggplot(enrichmentTop20, aes( y = fct_reorder(term_name, score), x = score, color = score, size = score )) + geom_point() + scale_color_gradientn( colours = c("#56A443", "#8AA443", "#f7ca64"), trans = "log10", guide = guide_colorbar(reverse = FALSE, order = 1) ) + scale_size_continuous(range = c(4, 8)) + theme_bw(base_size = 12) + xlab("score -log10(adj pvalue)") + ylab(NULL) + ggtitle("Pathway Enrichment Analysis") + theme( axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10) ) p Step 4 - Hierarchical Cluster The problem with the earlier visualization, which represents the top 20 pathways, is that it does not account for the overlap between gene sets. As you can observe, many pathways have similar names because they share a substantial number of genes. To provide a more accurate and efficient representation of the results, and to obtain a quicker and clearer overview, it would be more appropriate to aggregate and summarize pathways with substantial gene overlap, thereby reducing redundancy. Our first approach is to use hierarchical clustering based on a distance matrix that measures the similarity between pathways according to the number of genes they have in common, allowing us to visualize their relationships. enrichment_results_UPgenes <- gprofiler_results_custom_max500_UPgenes$result enrichment_results_UPgenes$score = -log10(as.numeric(enrichment_results_UPgenes$p_value)) # Top 20 enriched terms enrichmentTop20 <- enrichment_results_UPgenes %>% arrange(desc(score)) %>% slice_head(n = 20) Calculating the distance matrix using the jaccard coefficient Many pathways share genes, so similar biological processes can appear under different pathway names. To group similar pathways, we look at how many genes they have in common. The Jaccard coefficient measures the shared genes relative to all unique genes in the two pathways, from 0 (no overlap) to 1 (identical). The overlap coefficient measures the shared genes relative to the smaller pathway and shows when one pathway is mostly contained within another, from 0 (no overlap) to 1 (smaller pathway contained into larger one). Figure 3: Jaccard and overlap coefficients for two gene sets. We convert these scores into distances (1 − score) and use them to group similar pathways into broader biological themes. ##Illustration with Jaccard Coefficient # Convert genes to lists # (the intersection column, returned by g:Profiler with evcodes = TRUE, contains # the genes of our list found in each pathway, separated by a comma) gene_lists <- strsplit(enrichment_results_UPgenes$intersection, ",") # Calculate Jaccard similarity matrix n <- length(gene_lists) jaccard_mat <- matrix(0, n, n) rownames(jaccard_mat) <- enrichment_results_UPgenes$term_name colnames(jaccard_mat) <- enrichment_results_UPgenes$term_name for (i in seq_len(n)) { for (j in seq_len(n)) { intersection <- length(intersect(gene_lists[[i]], gene_lists[[j]])) union <- length(union(gene_lists[[i]], gene_lists[[j]])) jaccard_mat[i, j] <- intersection / union } } labs <- enrichment_results_UPgenes$term_name labs <- ifelse(nchar(labs) > 30, paste0(substr(labs, 1, 27), "..."), labs) rownames(jaccard_mat) <- colnames(jaccard_mat) <- make.unique(labs) keep <- sample(seq_len(nrow(jaccard_mat)), min(20, nrow(jaccard_mat))) jaccard_sub <- jaccard_mat[keep, keep] # Heatmap p <- pheatmap( jaccard_sub, color = colorRampPalette(c("white", "#C6DBEF", "#6BAED6", "#2171B5", "#08306B"))(100), breaks = seq(0, 1, length.out = 101), display_numbers = F, #number_format = "%.2f", #number_color = "black", #fontsize_number = 8, clustering_distance_rows = as.dist(1 - jaccard_sub), clustering_distance_cols = as.dist(1 - jaccard_sub), border_color = "grey90", fontsize_row = 7, fontsize_col = 7, angle_col = 45, main = "Jaccard coefficient (20 random gene sets)" ) ##Illustration with Overlap Coefficient # Calculate Overlap coefficient matrix (reuses gene_lists and n from above) overlap_mat <- matrix(0, n, n) for (i in seq_len(n)) { for (j in seq_len(n)) { intersection <- length(intersect(gene_lists[[i]], gene_lists[[j]])) smaller <- min(length(gene_lists[[i]]), length(gene_lists[[j]])) overlap_mat[i, j] <- intersection / smaller } } rownames(overlap_mat) <- colnames(overlap_mat) <- make.unique(labs) # Use the same 20 gene sets as the Jaccard heatmap so the two can be compared overlap_sub <- overlap_mat[keep, keep] # Heatmap p <- pheatmap( overlap_sub, color = colorRampPalette(c("white", "#C6DBEF", "#6BAED6", "#2171B5", "#08306B"))(100), breaks = seq(0, 1, length.out = 101), display_numbers = F, clustering_distance_rows = as.dist(1 - overlap_sub), clustering_distance_cols = as.dist(1 - overlap_sub), border_color = "grey90", fontsize_row = 7, fontsize_col = 7, angle_col = 45, main = "Overlap coefficient (20 random gene sets)" ) ##Hierarchical Clustering plot_hclust_enrichment: helper function to cluster the top enriched pathways by gene overlap (Jaccard distance) and plot them next to the dendrogram plot_hclust_enrichment = function(enrichment_results, n_top = 20, n_clusters = 8) { enrichment_results$score <- -log10(as.numeric(enrichment_results$p_value)) # Top n_top enriched terms enrichmentTop <- enrichment_results %>% arrange(desc(score)) %>% slice_head(n = n_top) top_terms <- enrichmentTop %>% arrange(as.numeric(p_value)) # Jaccard similarity matrix # (the intersection column contains the genes of our list found in each pathway) gene_lists <- strsplit(top_terms$intersection, ",") n <- length(gene_lists) jaccard_mat <- matrix(0, n, n, dimnames = list(top_terms$term_name, top_terms$term_name)) for (i in seq_len(n)) { for (j in seq_len(n)) { inter <- length(intersect(gene_lists[[i]], gene_lists[[j]])) uni <- length(union(gene_lists[[i]], gene_lists[[j]])) jaccard_mat[i, j] <- inter / uni } } # Hierarchical clustering dist_mat <- as.dist(1 - jaccard_mat) hc <- hclust(dist_mat, method = "average") term_order <- hc$labels[hc$order] # The first level is drawn at the bottom of the bar plot, matching the # first dendrogram leaf (y = 1) top_terms$term_name <- factor(top_terms$term_name, levels = term_order) top_terms$neglog10p <- -log10(as.numeric(top_terms$p_value)) # Cut tree into k branches (cannot have more branches than terms) k <- min(n_clusters, n) clusters <- cutree(hc, k = k) top_terms$cluster <- factor(clusters[as.character(top_terms$term_name)]) # Bar plot (full, coloured by cluster) base_colours <- c("#1D9E75", "#3A7DC9", "#E07B39", "#9B59B6", "#E74C3C", "#F1C40F", "#1ABC9C", "#E91E63") # Interpolate extra colours when more than 8 clusters are requested if (k <= length(base_colours)) { cluster_colours <- base_colours } else { cluster_colours <- colorRampPalette(base_colours)(k) } p_bar <- ggplot(top_terms, aes(x = neglog10p, y = term_name, fill = cluster)) + geom_col(alpha = 0.85, width = 0.7) + scale_y_discrete(expand = c(0, 0.5)) + scale_fill_manual(values = cluster_colours[seq_len(k)], name = "Branch") + labs(x = expression(-log[10](p-value)), y = NULL) + theme_bw(base_size = 10) + theme( panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), axis.text.y = element_text(size = 8), legend.position = "right" ) # Dendrogram dend_data <- dendro_data(hc, type = "rectangle") seg <- dend_data$segments p_dend <- ggplot(seg) + geom_segment(aes(x = y, y = x, xend = yend, yend = xend), colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.45) + scale_x_reverse(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0))) + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0.5, n + 0.5), expand = c(0, 0)) + labs(x = "Jaccard distance") + theme_void() + theme( axis.title.x = element_text(size = 8, colour = "grey50", margin = margin(t = 4)), axis.text.x = element_text(size = 7, colour = "grey60"), plot.margin = margin(0, 4, 0, 0) ) # Combined plot p_combined <- p_dend + p_bar + plot_layout(widths = c(3, 1)) # Keep only the top hit per branch top_per_cluster <- top_terms %>% group_by(cluster) %>% slice_min(as.numeric(p_value), n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>% ungroup() %>% arrange(as.numeric(p_value)) %>% mutate(term_name = factor(as.character(term_name), levels = rev(as.character(term_name)))) # Simple barplot — one representative term per branch p_simple <- ggplot(top_per_cluster, aes(x = neglog10p, y = term_name, fill = cluster)) + geom_col(alpha = 0.88, width = 0.6) + geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("p = %.2e", as.numeric(p_value))), hjust = -0.1, size = 3, colour = "grey30") + scale_fill_manual(values = cluster_colours[seq_len(k)], name = "Branch") + scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.25))) + labs( x = expression(-log[10](p-value)), y = NULL, title = "Top term per branch" ) + theme_bw(base_size = 11) + theme( panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9), legend.position = "bottom", plot.title = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold") ) # n_terms and n_clusters are returned so the figure height can be set # from them in the chunk options return(list(combined = p_combined, top_per_branch = p_simple, n_terms = n, n_clusters = k)) } Running the function on the top 20 pathways enrichment_results_UPgenes <- gprofiler_results_custom_max500_UPgenes$result hc_plots <- plot_hclust_enrichment(enrichment_results = enrichment_results_UPgenes, n_top = 20, n_clusters = 10) The figure height grows with the number of pathways (combined plot) and the number of clusters (top term per branch), so the bars do not overlap. hc_plots$combined hc_plots$top_per_branch YOUR TURN Running the function with your defined number of pathways and clusters NOTE: In the next module, you will learn a better approach to address redundancy and visualize enriched gene sets as networks using Cytoscape and EnrichmentMap.

Authors: Veronique Voisin, Ruth Isserlin Presenter: Veronique Voisin Introduction This practical lab contains one exercise. It uses fGSEA to perform a gene-set enrichment analysis. Goal of the exercise Learn how to run fGSEA and explore the results. Data We will perform gene-set enrichment analysis using the output of the differential expression analysis comparing the palbo-resistant and the MCF7 parental cell line. We won’t use only the signficant differentially expressed genes but we will rank all genes from top up-regulated to down-regulated. The non significant genes stays in the rank file. Background The goal of this lab is to: Upload the 2 required files into GSEA, Adjust relevant parameters, Run fGSEA, Open and explore the gene-set enrichment results. The 2 required files are: a rank file (.rnk) a pathway definition file (.gmt). Rank File To generate a rank file (.rnk), a score (-log10(pvalue) * sign(logFC)) was calculated from the edgeR differential expression results. A gene that is significantly differentially expressed (i.e associated with a very small pvalue, close to 0) will be assigned a high score.The sign of the logFC indicates if the gene has an expression which is higher in Palbo-resistant (logFC > 0, the score will have a + sign) or higher in Parental (logFC < 0, the score will have a - sign). It is used to rank the genes from top up-regulated to top down-regulated (all genes have to be included). Exercise 1 - prepare the gene lists This exercise requires the file “edgeR_resistant_vs_parental_all_genes.csv” located in the data folder. Step 1 - Install and Load libraries # CRAN and Bioconductor setup if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("BiocManager") # List of CRAN packages cran_packages <- c( "tidyverse", "knitr", "kableExtra", "glue", "ggridges", "data.table" ) # List of Bioconductor packages bioc_packages <- c( "fgsea", "clusterProfiler", "enrichplot" ) # Install CRAN packages if not already installed for (pkg in cran_packages) { if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) { install.packages(pkg) } } # Install Bioconductor packages if not already installed for (pkg in bioc_packages) { if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) { BiocManager::install(pkg) } } # Load the libraries library(tidyverse) library(knitr) library(kableExtra) library(glue) library(ggridges) library(data.table) # Bioconductor packages library(fgsea) library(clusterProfiler) library(enrichplot) # create the results folder (if it does not exist yet) to save the outputs # dir.create("results", showWarnings = FALSE) # Location of the Module 8 files (data/, BYODdata/, image/): # - on the course server: ~/CourseData/Module8 # - when the book is built from the repository: Module8 data_dir <- if (dir.exists("~/CourseData/Module8")) "~/CourseData/Module8" else "Module8" Step 2 - Prepare the rank file , upload the gmt file and run fgsea fGSEA is an R package that runs a fast Gene Set Enrichment Analysis. In the below command the following options have been specified: pathways - list of genesets to use for the calculation stats - genes and their associated statistic, sorted ( rank file) max_size - maximum size for individual gene sets. min_size - minimum size for individual gene sets gseaParam - GSEA parameter value gseaParam - GSEA parameter value. All ranks will be raised to this power when calculating the ES scores. Equivalent to the weight in the original GSEA algorithm. res = read.csv(file.path(data_dir, "data/edgeR_resistant_vs_parental_all_genes.csv")) gmtfile = file.path(data_dir, "data/Human_GOBP_AllPathways_noPFOCR_no_GO_iea_September_14_2026_symbol.gmt") pathways <- fgsea::gmtPathways(gmtfile) ## rank file formatted for gsea ranks <- setNames(res$score, res$gene) ranks <- ranks[!is.na(ranks) & !is.na(names(ranks))] ranks <- sort(ranks, decreasing = TRUE) set.seed(543) ## to get reproducible results ## running fgsea fgseaRes <- fgsea( pathways = pathways, stats = ranks, minSize = 10, maxSize = 500, nperm = 2000 ) ## Warning in fgsea(pathways = pathways, stats = ranks, minSize = 10, maxSize = ## 500, : You are trying to run fgseaSimple. It is recommended to use ## fgseaMultilevel. To run fgseaMultilevel, you need to remove the nperm argument ## in the fgsea function call. ## Warning in preparePathwaysAndStats(pathways, stats, minSize, maxSize, gseaParam, : There are ties in the preranked stats (0.01% of the list). ## The order of those tied genes will be arbitrary, which may produce unexpected results. fgseaRes <- fgseaRes[order(fgseaRes$padj), ] Save the full fgsea results table to the results folder. #the leadingEdge column is a list of genes for each pathway, #convert it to text (genes separated by a comma) so that it can be written to a csv file. fgseaRes_to_save <- copy(fgseaRes) fgseaRes_to_save$leadingEdge <- sapply(fgseaRes_to_save$leadingEdge, paste, collapse = ",") # write.csv(fgseaRes_to_save, "results/fgsea_results_resistant_vs_parental.csv", row.names = FALSE) Set gseaParam to 2 if you want to add more weight on the most top up-regulated and top down-regulated. 2 is a more stringent parameter and it will result in less gene-sets significant under FDR <0.05. A small number (a few hundred genesets if using baderlab genesets) could indicate an issue with identifier mapping. Check the number of sets that have FDR less than 0.25 – in order to determine what thresholds to start with when creating the enrichment map. It is not uncommon to see a thousand gene sets pass the threshold of FDR less than 0.25. FDR less than 0.25 is a very lax threshold and for robust data we can set thresholds of FDR less than 0.05 or lower. Install and load libraries ## CRAN and Bioconductor setup if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("BiocManager") ## List of CRAN packages cran_packages <- c( "tidyverse", "ggrepel" ) # List of Bioconductor packages bioc_packages <- c( "edgeR" ) # Install CRAN packages if not already installed for (pkg in cran_packages) { if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) { install.packages(pkg) } } # Install Bioconductor packages if not already installed for (pkg in bioc_packages) { if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) { BiocManager::install(pkg) } } # Load the libraries # CRAN packages library(tidyverse) library(ggrepel) # Bioconductor packages library(edgeR) # create the results folder (if it does not exist yet) to save the outputs # dir.create("results", showWarnings = FALSE) # Location of the Module 8 files (data/, BYODdata/, image/): # - on the course server: ~/CourseData/Module8 # - when the book is built from the repository: Module8 data_dir <- if (dir.exists("~/CourseData/Module8")) "~/CourseData/Module8" else "Module8" Data used for this comparison For this analysis, we are going to compare the Palbo-resistant cell lines (MCF7 1.2 Palbo-resistant, 3 biological replicates) versus the Abema-resistant cell lines (MCF7 0.5 Abema-resistant, 3 biological replicates). The count files are in the BYODdata folder. Figure 4: GEO dataset (GSE222367): samples used for the Palbo-resistant vs Abema-resistant comparison generate a DGE object # 1. Find the count files files <- list.files(path = file.path(data_dir, "BYODdata"), pattern = "\\.txt\\.gz$", full.names = TRUE) # 2. Sample names from the file names (strip the extension) samples <- sub("_S.*", "", basename(files)) # 3. Read the files into a DGEList # HTSeq output has no header: column 1 = gene ID, column 2 = count. # R reads gzipped files directly, so no need to decompress. dge <- readDGE(files, columns = c(1, 2), header = FALSE, labels = samples) ## Meta tags detected: __no_feature, __ambiguous, __too_low_aQual, __not_aligned, __alignment_not_unique # 4. Remove HTSeq summary rows (__no_feature, __ambiguous, etc.) dge <- dge[!grepl("^__", rownames(dge)), , keep.lib.sizes = FALSE] # 5. (Optional) add group information # files are listed in this order: GSM6921640-42 (Palbo-resistant), # then GSM6921655-57 (Abema-resistant) dge$samples$group <- factor( c("palbo_resistant", "palbo_resistant", "palbo_resistant", "abema_resistant", "abema_resistant", "abema_resistant"), levels = c("abema_resistant", "palbo_resistant") # abema_resistant = reference ) # check that each sample has the right group dge$samples[, c("files", "group")] ## files ## GSM6921640 Module8/BYODdata/GSM6921640_S1M712_P.htseqcount.txt.gz ## GSM6921641 Module8/BYODdata/GSM6921641_S5M712_P.htseqcount.txt.gz ## GSM6921642 Module8/BYODdata/GSM6921642_S6M712_P.htseqcount.txt.gz ## Genes retained after filtering: 13488 mds <- plotMDS(dge, col = as.numeric(dge$samples$group), main = "MDS (logCPM)") group = dge$samples$group var_pct <- round(100 * mds$var.explained[mds$dim.plot]) mds_df <- data.frame(dim1 = mds$x, dim2 = mds$y, sample = colnames(dge), group = group) ggplot(mds_df, aes(x = dim1, y = dim2, color = group)) + geom_point(size = 3) + ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = sample), size = 3, color = "grey30", show.legend = FALSE, max.overlaps = Inf, box.padding = 0.4, segment.color = "grey60") + labs(title = "MDS plot (all samples)", x = sprintf("Leading logFC dim %d (%d%%)", mds$dim.plot[1], var_pct[1]), y = sprintf("Leading logFC dim %d (%d%%)", mds$dim.plot[2], var_pct[2]), color = "Group") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "right") Design (~0 + group) and named contrast design <- model.matrix(~ 0 + group, data = dge$samples) colnames(design) <- levels(dge$samples$group) # "abema_resistant", "palbo_resistant" contr <- makeContrasts( palbo_resistant_vs_abema_resistant = palbo_resistant - abema_resistant, # + logFC = up in Palbo-resistant levels = design ) head(design) ##
