This means that you are able to copy, share and modify the work, as long as the result is distributed under the same license. By Gary Bader, Ruth Isserlin, Veronique Voisin Goal of the exercise Create a network and customize it. The goal of this exercise is to learn how to create a network in Cytoscape and customize id. In this example, the proteins are the entities represented as nodes in the network and known physical interactions are the connections between the proteins that are represented as edges. We will overlay 2 additional pieces of information about these proteins, mutation information per protein as node color and mutation expression as node size. Data The data used in this exercise is a set of protein - protein interactions and associated attributes. Start the exercise To start the lab practical section, first create a cytoscape_primer_files directoty on your computer and download the files below. Right click on link below and select “Save Link As…”. Place it in the corresponding module directory of your CBW work directory. Two files are needed for this exercise: networktable.txt nodeattribute.txt Exercise 1a - Create Network from table Launch Cytoscape Locate the top menu bar and select File,–> Import, –> Network from File…. Browse your computer and select the file networktable.txt An Import Network from Table dialog box opens. The 3 columns of the table should be set as “source”, “interaction” and “target” respectively. Cytoscape will assume, by default, will look for the column names that start with “source”, “interaction” and “target”. It will assume that any other column is an interaction attribute (edge attribute) This is just an example file. You can import files with any number of additional columns and choose to ignore all columns except for the ones that you want to import or import all of them. Although Cytoscape tries to guess the data type of each column and the type (ie. is it an attribute associated with source node, target nodes or the interaction) you are able to fine tune everything. Click “Ok”. A network containing the proteins as blue square nodes and interaction as edges should be displayed in the main Cytoscape window. Equivalent RCy3 code — Create network from a table file Setting up cytoscape variables - The values of the below variables depends on where you are running your R Code and where you are running your Cytoscape. There are a lot of different combinations but it is important to understand your set up. Almost always you will be running cytoscape on your computer or laptop. Something that you can interact with directly. But often we might run our code on: A Docker on your computer A docker on a remote machine AWS cloud another cloud service. When we send commands to cytoscape we need to specify where cytoscape is. We have defined a variable that we will use for every command we send to cytoscape telling it where the cytoscape host is: 1. From RStudio on your computer to cytoscape on your computer - current_cytoscape_baseurl = “http://localhost:1234/v1” 1. From docker implementation of Rstudio on your computer to cytoscape on your computer - current_cytoscape_baseurl = “http://host.docker.internal:1234/v1” 1. From AWS Rstudio to cytoscape on your computer - a. Set up ssh tunnel from your computer to AWS as follows - ssh -i <studentname>.pem -R 1234:localhost:1234 ubuntu@can.uhn-hpc.ca a. current_cytoscape_baseurl = "http://localhost:1234/v1" When cytoscape loads or saves files, it can not save to the docker or the cloud. It only has access to the files on the computer that it is running. So the path to files saved or accessed by cytoscape need to be on the machine that is running cytoscape. Initialize the variable to a directory on your computer that you want to save all your results path_to_save_cytoscape = “/Users/risserlin/CBW_Workshop_results/Module9” library(RCy3) is_remote = TRUE current_cytoscape_baseurl = "http://host.docker.internal:1234/v1" #make sure this directory is created ahead of time. We can't create this directory from this instance of RStudio. path_to_save_cytoscape = "/Users/risserlin/CBW_Workshop_results/Module9" # Confirm Cytoscape is running and reachable cytoscapePing(base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) # Read the network table into R network_df <- read.table( "./Module9/cytoscape_primer/data/network_table.txt", header = TRUE, sep = "\t", stringsAsFactors = FALSE ) # The table has columns: source, interaction, target # createNetworkFromDataFrames() takes a separate edges data frame and # an optional nodes data frame. Here we build edges directly from the table. edges_df <- data.frame( source = network_df$source, target = network_df$target, interaction = network_df$interaction, stringsAsFactors = FALSE ) # Create the network in Cytoscape network_suid <- createNetworkFromDataFrames( edges = edges_df, title = "Cytoscape Primer Network", collection = "Module 9", base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl ) # Confirm the network was created message("Network SUID: ", network_suid) Exercise 1b - Load node attributes Locate the Cytoscape top menu bar and select File,–> Import,–> Table from File…. Browse your computer and select the file nodeattribute.txt click “Open”. An “Import Table from Columns” dialog appears. Click on “OK”. You should be able to see the imported attributes in the node table. The key column is assumed to be the first column in your table. The key is the column in the loaded attribute file used to match your attributes to your network. key column for Network is the column in the Network that the key is matched to. (In this network there isn’t the ability to set this value because that is the only attribute associated with the nodes in our network but normally this drop box will be selectable) The key and matching column need to match perfectly (unless you have specified that case does not matter). Similar to the Import Network from Table, everything about the import is customizable. Cytoscape does its best to guess the datatypes of each column but you are able to fine tune it. There are also advanced options if you want to: change the file delimiter skip lines specify the header column Equivalent RCy3 code — Load node attributes from a file # Read the node attribute table into R node_attributes <- read.table( "./Module9/cytoscape_primer/data/node_attribute.txt", header = TRUE, sep = "\t", stringsAsFactors = FALSE ) # loadTableData() merges the data frame into the Cytoscape node table. # The 'data.key.column' is the column in node_attributes that matches # the node name column in Cytoscape (default: "name"). loadTableData( data = node_attributes, data.key.column = colnames(node_attributes)[1], # first column is the key table = "node", table.key.column = "name", network = network_suid, base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl ) message("Node attributes loaded successfully.") Exercise 1c - Map node attributes to Visual Style Go to “Control Panel” on the left side and select the “Style” tab. Make sure that you are in the “Node” tab. Select the “Fill Color” field expand it by clicking on the right arrow. Set “Column” to “expression” and “Mapping Type” to “Continuous Mapping”. This will change the colours of the nodes to the default colour coding. Double click on the continuos mapping colour box to manually adjust the colour and other settings. At the bottom of the “Style” tab, check the box “Lock node width and height”. Select the “Size” field and expand it by clicking on the right arrow. Set “Column” to “mutation” and “Mapping Type” to “Continuous Mapping”. Your resulting network maps expression to the colour of the node and the size of the node to the number of mutations. Adjust the setting on the colour mapping. Change the colour scheme. Change the maximum and minimum values. Adjust the setting on the size mapping. Make the nodes bigger with higher values. Even though the network is small, play around with the layouts. Equivalent RCy3 code — Map node attributes to visual properties # ── Colour: map 'expression' column to node fill colour ───────────────────── # Set a continuous colour mapping: low expression = blue, mid = white, high = red # First get the range of the expression values from the node table node_table_current <- getTableColumns(table = "node", network = network_suid,base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) expr_min <- min(node_table_current$expression, na.rm = TRUE) expr_max <- max(node_table_current$expression, na.rm = TRUE) expr_mid <- (expr_min + expr_max) / 2 setNodeColorMapping( table.column = "expression", table.column.values = c(expr_min, expr_mid, expr_max), colors = c("#0000FF", "#FFFFFF", "#FF0000"), # blue -> white -> red mapping.type = "continuous", network = network_suid, base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl ) # ── Size: map 'mutation' column to node size ────────────────────────────────── mut_min <- min(node_table_current$mutation, na.rm = TRUE) mut_max <- max(node_table_current$mutation, na.rm = TRUE) setNodeSizeMapping( table.column = "mutation", table.column.values = c(mut_min, mut_max), sizes = c(30, 100), # smallest to largest node size in pixels mapping.type = "continuous", network = network_suid, base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl ) # Lock node width and height so size mapping applies uniformly lockNodeDimensions(TRUE, base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) message("Visual style mappings applied.") Exercise 2 - Work with larger networks Cytoscape supplies a few demo networks that you can play around with. When you open cytoscape you are presented with a Start Panel where you can choose to reload a previous session or load in one of the sample networks. You do not need to re-open cytoscape to open the starter panel. Locate the Cytoscape top menu bar and select View,–> Show Starter panel. Double click on the Affinity Purification Network to open it. If you already have a session open then you will receive a warning that the current session will be lost. Before proceeding make sure your current session is saved. (Click on cancel. Then, File –> Save as) Once the network has loaded you will see a network of protein interactions derived from an affinity purification experiment. Bait proteins are represented as pink hexagons and their corresponding prey proteins blue boxes. Using this larger network play around with the different layouts Search for the node “VPR” select all of the prey proteins associated with “VPR” Equivalent RCy3 code — Save current session, open a sample network, apply layouts, search for a node and select its neighbours Save current session before moving onto the next example - This is a little bit difficult because cytoscape is running on your computer but you are running this code from your instance which is in the cloud. the path to the file from within the instance is not the same as the one that cytoscape will see on your computer. # ── Save the current session before switching networks ─────────────────────── saveSession(filename = file.path(path_to_save_cytoscape, "my_session.cys"), base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) # ── Open the Affinity Purification sample network ──────────────────────────── # Cytoscape ships sample sessions in its installation directory. # The easiest way via RCy3 is to open the session file directly if you know # its path, or to use the openSession command: openSession( file.location = file.path( Sys.getenv("CYTOSCAPE_HOME", "/Applications/Cytoscape_v3.10.5"), "sampleData", "sessions", "Affinity Purification.cys" ), base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl ) # Get the SUID of the newly loaded network ap_suid <- getNetworkSuid(base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) # ── Try different layouts ───────────────────────────────────────────────────── # List available layout algorithms getLayoutNames(base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) # Apply a force-directed layout layoutNetwork("force-directed", network = ap_suid, base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) # Apply a hierarchical layout layoutNetwork("hierarchical", network = ap_suid, base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) # ── Search for the node "VPR" and select its first neighbours ──────────────── # Select VPR by name selectNodes(nodes = "VPR", by.col = "name", network = ap_suid, base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) # Expand selection to include all directly connected (first-neighbour) nodes selectFirstNeighbors(network = ap_suid, base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) # Retrieve the names of all currently selected nodes selected <- getSelectedNodes(network = ap_suid, base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) message("Selected nodes: ", paste(selected, collapse = ", ")) Exercise 3 - Perform basic enrichment analysis using EnrichmentTable In Module 8 we performed detailed enrichment analysis with g:profiler and GSEA. We supplied gene lists and ranked expression sets in order to perform the analysis. What if you want to run a quick enrichment analysis with a given network or a given subset of the network? The easiest way to do this is to use the cytoscape app EnrichmentTable. EnrichmentTable will query g:profiler directly with the given network or subnetwork. Not all of the parameters that are available in the web version can be tweaked from the enrichmentmap table app but it can be an easy way to quickly see enrichment results. We will select the bait protein VPR and all its associated prey proteins to use for an enrichment analysis. Bait Protein - Is the labelled protein in an affinity purification experiment that is pulled down. Prey Protein - are the proteins that are associated with the bait protein when it is pulled down and are assumed to interact with the bait protein. First neighbor - are all the nodes that are directly connected to the given node 1. In the search bar enter “VPR”. Press enter. VPR is now the only highlighted node in the network. In order to select all its associated preys we need to select all the nodes that are connected to VPR, all of VPR’s first neighbours. There are two ways to select the first neighbours: In the top menu bar click on Select –> Nodes –> First neighbors of selected nodes –> undirected Click on the first neighbor button, , in the quick links button set. Click on the “Enrichment Table” in the Table Panel. If the Enrichment Table tab is not in the Table Panel, Open Enrichment Table. Go to: Tools –> Enrichment Table –> Perform Gene Enrichment to launch Enrichment Table Tab. Click on the cog icon in the top right hand corner of the Enrichment Table panel This will bring up a panel with the adjustable settings. There are only 5 adjustable parameters- Organism - This shows a list of organisms that are available on the g:Profiler site. Gene ID column - the column in the current network that you want to use to search g:Profiler with. Ideally this should be a column specifying the Gene Name or other identifier. Multiple testing correction - change to fdr. Adjusted p-value threshold (min 0 max 1) - leave as 0.05. If you are getting too many results you can make this value smaller. Include inferred GO annotations (IEA) - by default the search will exclude inferred from electronic annotation GO terms. If you want to include them, select this option. By default, EnrichmentTable automatically uses all the databases available on the g:Profiler site. There is no way to filter prior to running the analysis. You need to filter the results after the analysis has been run. This will change the results because you end up filtering the results after the multiple correction and the multiple correction is dependent on the number of genesets you are testing with. Filter the EnrichmentTable results to show only GO:BP, Reactome and Wikipathway, similar to what we used in Module 2. Click on the filter icon in the top left hand corner of the enrichment table results. Next to Select Categories select Gene Ontology Biological Process, Reactome, Wikipathways. To select multiple options click and hold command key on Mac or Shift on Windows. click on OK The EnrichmentTable will update to only include the sets from Gene Ontology Biological Process, Reactome, Wikipathways. Equivalent RCy3 code — Select VPR and its first neighbours, then run g:Profiler enrichment directly from R library(gprofiler2) # ── Select VPR and its first neighbours ────────────────────────────────────── selectNodes(nodes = "VPR", by.col = "name", network = ap_suid, base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) selectFirstNeighbors(network = ap_suid, base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) # Get the names of all selected nodes (VPR + prey proteins) vpr_neighbourhood <- getSelectedNodes(network = ap_suid, base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) message("Nodes in VPR neighbourhood: ", length(vpr_neighbourhood)) # ── Run g:Profiler enrichment directly from R ───────────────────────────────── # This replicates what EnrichmentTable does internally, with full control over # all parameters including source filtering before multiple testing correction. gp_results <- gost( query = vpr_neighbourhood, organism = "hsapiens", correction_method = "fdr", user_threshold = 0.05, evcodes = TRUE, # include evidence codes (like IEA filter) sources = c("GO:BP", "REAC", "WP") # GO:BP, Reactome, WikiPathways ) # View the top results if (!is.null(gp_results)) { results_df <- gp_results$result results_df <- results_df[order(results_df$p_value), ] print(head(results_df[, c("term_name", "source", "p_value", "term_size", "intersection_size")], 20)) } else { message("No significant enrichment results found.") } Exercise 3B - create Enrichment Map and Enhanced graphics nodes from EnrichmentTable To create an Enrichment Map from the EnrichmentTable results, Click on the EM logo in the top left hand bar in the ErichmentTable Panel. This will bring up an EM options panel with very limited parameter adjustments. You can only change the name of the network and the connectivity threshold. You have already specified the p-value threshold when you originally performed the analysis. If you want to create your network with a more permissive q-value you need to go back to the EnrichmentTable search panel. Click on OK This will create an Enrichment Map in a new network and represents all the Gene Ontology Biological Process, Reactome, Wikipathways terms enriched for the VPR and its prey protein set. Equivalent RCy3 code — Build an Enrichment Map from g:Profiler results using the EnrichmentMap Cytoscape app Cytoscape has no access to the files that we create on the instance or remote server. We need to upload the file to Cytoscape so it can see it. #if using docker we need to replace all the the paths to the host path if(is_remote) { upload_em_file <- function(localPath) { # EnrichmentMap's upload endpoint is on the root port, #not under /v1 base_no_v1 <- sub("/v1$", "", current_cytoscape_baseurl) bname <- basename(localPath) r <- httr::POST( url = paste(base_no_v1, '/enrichmentmap/textfileupload?fileName=', bname, sep=""), config = list(), body = list(file = httr::upload_file(localPath)), encode = "multipart", handle = NULL ) httr::content(r,"parsed")$path } } library(RCy3) # ── Write g:Profiler results to a file that EnrichmentMap can read ──────────── # EnrichmentMap accepts g:Profiler results via its file-based input. # gprofiler2::gost() can write a GMT-compatible file directly. em_dir <- "./Module9/cytoscape_primer/em_output" dir.create(em_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE) gp_gem_file <- file.path(em_dir, "vpr_gprofiler.gem.txt") # Write the g:Profiler results in the Generic Enrichment Map (GEM) format if (!is.null(gp_results)) { gem_df <- data.frame( Name = gp_results$result$term_name, Description = gp_results$result$term_id, pvalue = gp_results$result$p_value, qvalue = gp_results$result$p_value, # gost returns fdr-corrected p_value phenotype = 1, genes = sapply(gp_results$result$intersection, paste, collapse = ","), stringsAsFactors = FALSE ) write.table(gem_df, file = gp_gem_file, sep = "\t", quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE, col.names = TRUE) } #if cytoscape is remote then upload the file we just created if(is_remote) { gp_gem_file <- upload_em_file(gp_gem_file) } # ── Build the Enrichment Map via the RCy3 / EM command interface ────────────── # Use commandsRun() to call the EnrichmentMap build command directly em_command <- paste( "enrichmentmap build", paste0("analysisType=", "generic"), paste0("enrichmentsDataset1=", gp_gem_file), paste0("pvalue=", "1.0"), # already filtered by gost; keep all paste0("qvalue=", "0.05"), paste0("coefficients=", "COMBINED"), paste0("similaritycutoff=", "0.375"), sep = " " ) commandsRun(em_command,base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) message("Enrichment Map created from VPR neighbourhood g:Profiler results.") Exercise 4 - Load network from NDex NDex is an open-source repository where scientists can store, share, manipulate and publish biological network data. Networks are viewable on the web through their webapp but can also be downloaded directly into cytoscape so you can search, manipulate, integrate and analyze the given network for yourselves. For the purpose of this exercise we are going to load in a network from the publication A protein landscape of Breast Cancer. This publication is associated with multiple networks the the authors of this paper created and shared in NDex - https://www.ndexbio.org/index.html#/networkset/4423340d-e8e3-11eb-b666-0ac135e8bacf Start a new session. File –> Close In the Network Search bar (located at the top of the control panel) make sure that the search provider is set to NDex. It should be set to NDex by default but click on down arrow to see the different data sources you can search for. Later in the workshop we will be using this bar to query GeneMania. Enter MCF7_All_PPI>=0.9 into the search box, Click on the search icon. A search results box will appear. The MCF7_All_PPI>=0.9 network is just one of the networks associated with this publication. Eventhough you are searching for this specific network, other networks associated with the original paper will also show up in the search results as well as others. Click on the green down arrow next to MCF7_All_PPI>=0.9, the network will start to import. Once the network has been loaded, click on Close Dialog Resulting network loaded into cytoccape. Description taken from NDex record Baits are shown as yellow box, and preys as grey circle. Size of each node represents number of patients with alterations in each protein. Dotted line represents the physical protein-protein association (validated in other studies) with high Integrated Association Stringency score. Change the edge width to reflect the number of patients the associations is found in instead of the PPI score. Change the default node colour to blue. Equivalent RCy3 code — Close current session, import a network from NDEx, and apply bonus visual style changes library(RCy3) library(ndexr) # install with: BiocManager::install("ndexr") # ── Close current session ───────────────────────────────────────────────────── closeSession(save.before.closing = FALSE, base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) # ── Import the MCF7_All_PPI>=0.9 network from NDEx ─────────────────────────── # The NDEx UUID for this network (from the publication's NDEx record) mcf7_ndex_uuid <- "84e36f91-ecb7-11eb-b666-0ac135e8bacf" # Import directly into Cytoscape via the CyNDEx2 app command # (requires the CyNDEx2 Cytoscape app to be installed) importNetworkFromNDEx(ndex.id = mcf7_ndex_uuid, base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) # Get the SUID of the imported network mcf7_suid <- getNetworkSuid(base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) message("MCF7 network SUID: ", mcf7_suid) # Apply a layout to make the network readable layoutNetwork("force-directed", network = mcf7_suid, base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) # ── BONUS: Change edge width to reflect number of patients ──────────────────── # First inspect the edge table to find the relevant column name edge_table <- getTableColumns(table = "edge", network = mcf7_suid, base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) print(colnames(edge_table)) # identify the patients column name #get current style current_style <- getCurrentStyle( base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) # Assuming the column is called "Npat" patient_col <- "Npat" # <-- update this to the actual column name patient_min <- min(edge_table[[patient_col]], na.rm = TRUE) patient_max <- max(edge_table[[patient_col]], na.rm = TRUE) setEdgeLineWidthMapping( table.column = patient_col, table.column.values = c(patient_min, patient_max), widths = c(1, 15), mapping.type = "continuous", network = mcf7_suid, style.name = current_style, base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl ) # ── BONUS: Change default node colour to blue ───────────────────────────────── setNodeColorDefault(new.color = "#4A90D9", style.name = current_style, base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) message("Visual style updates applied to MCF7 network.")

Module 9.2 Lab: g:profiler Visualization This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 3.0 Unported License. This means that you are able to copy, share and modify the work, as long as the result is distributed under the same license. By Gary Bader, Ruth Isserlin, Veronique Voisin Goal of the exercise Create an enrichment map and navigate through the network During this exercise, you will learn how to create an enrichment map from gene-set enrichment results. The enrichment results chosen for this exercise are generated using g:Profiler but an enrichment map can be created directly from output from: GSEA, g:Profiler, GREAT, BinGo, Enrichr or alternately from any gene-set tool using the generic enrichment results (GEM) format. Data The data used in this exercise is a differentially expressed gene set from palbociclib-resistant samples compared with parental samples from the breast cancer cell line MCF7 previous exercise. EnrichmentMap A circle (node) is a gene-set (pathway) enriched in genes that we used as input in g:Profiler (frequently mutated genes). edges (lines) represent genes in common between 2 pathways (nodes). A cluster of nodes represent overlapping and related pathways and may represent a common biological process. Clicking on a node will display the genes included in each pathway. Description of this exercise We will create EnrichmentMaps from: Two g:Profiler results run on UP- and DOWN-regulated genes separately . fgsea results using the Baderlab gene set file . An enrichment map represents the result of enrichment analysis as a network where significantly enriched gene-sets that share a lot of genes in common will form identifiable clusters. The visualization of the results as these biological themes will ease the interpretation of the results. The goal of this exercise is to learn how to: Upload g:Profiler results into Cytoscape EnrichmentMap to create a map. Upload UP and DOWN regulated g:Profiler results at the same time to create one combined map. Create an EnrichmentMap from fgsea results using the Baderlab gene set file. Start the exercise To start the lab practical section, first create a gprofiler_files directory on your computer and download the files below. Right click on link below and select “Save Link As…”. Place it in the corresponding module directory of your CBW work directory. Two input files are needed to generate all the enrichment results: Differential expression results: edgeR_resistant_vs_parental_all_genes.csv * Full edgeR output with columns: logFC, logCPM, F, PValue, FDR, gene, score Custom Baderlab gene set file: Human_GOBP_AllPathways_filtered_500orLessV2.gmt * Pre-filtered to gene sets with 500 or fewer genes enrichment_results_gprofiler_UPgenes.gem.txt — g:profiler UP genes results, GEM format for EnrichmentMap enrichment_results_gprofiler_DNgenes.gem.txt — g:profiler DOWN genes results, GEM format for EnrichmentMap gprofiler_full_hsapiens.name.gmt — downloaded from g:Profiler The Baderlab custom GMT (Human_GOBP_AllPathways_filtered_500orLessV2.gmt) is pre-filtered to gene sets with 500 or fewer genes, which means the FDR correction is applied only to those gene sets — giving more statistical power than filtering after the fact. evcodes = TRUE in the gost() call is required to get the intersection column, which contains the actual gene IDs from your query that overlap with each term. Despite the name, this is not GO evidence codes — it is the intersecting gene identifiers. RCy3 Setup — run once before all exercises library(RCy3) library(httr) library(jsonlite) path_to_save_cytoscape = "/Users/risserlin/CBW_Workshop_results/Module9" # Set base URL — adjust if not running from Docker current_cytoscape_baseurl <- "http://localhost:1234/v1" cytoscapePing(base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) cytoscapeVersionInfo(base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) # Helper: upload a local file to Cytoscape so EM can read it. # EnrichmentMap's upload endpoint sits outside /v1. upload_em_file <- function(localPath) { bname <- basename(localPath) base_no_v1 <- sub("/v1$", "", current_cytoscape_baseurl) r <- httr::POST( url = paste0(base_no_v1, "/enrichmentmap/textfileupload?fileName=", bname), config = list(), body = list(file = httr::upload_file(localPath)), encode = "multipart", handle = NULL ) jsonlite::fromJSON(rawToChar(r$content))$path } # Helper: convert fgsea CSV result to GEM format and write to disk. # g:Profiler GEM files are already written by the prepare-enrichment-files chunk. fgsea_csv_to_gem <- function(csv_path, gem_path) { fs <- read.csv(csv_path, stringsAsFactors = FALSE) gem <- data.frame( Name = fs$pathway, Description = fs$pathway, pvalue = fs$pval, qvalue = fs$padj, phenotype = ifelse(fs$NES >= 0, 1, -1), genes = fs$leadingEdge, stringsAsFactors = FALSE ) write.table(gem, file = gem_path, sep = "\t", quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE, col.names = TRUE) invisible(gem_path) } # ── File paths (g:Profiler GEMs written by prepare-enrichment-files chunk) ─── data_dir <- "./Module9/gprofiler/data" up_gem <- file.path(data_dir, "enrichment_results_gprofiler_UPgenes.gem.txt") dn_gem <- file.path(data_dir, "enrichment_results_gprofiler_DNgenes.gem.txt") fgsea_csv <- file.path(data_dir, "fgsea_resistant_vs_parental.csv") fgsea_gem <- file.path(data_dir, "fgsea_report_for_list.tsv") gmt_gprofiler <- file.path(data_dir, "gprofiler_full_hsapiens.name.gmt") gmt_baderlab <- file.path(data_dir, "Human_GOBP_AllPathways_filtered_500orLessV2.gmt") rnk_file <- file.path(data_dir, "resistant_vs_parental.rnk") message("Setup complete. All GEM files ready in: ", data_dir) Exercise 1a - compare UP and DOWN regulated g:Profiler results Step 1 Launch Cytoscape and open the EnrichmentMap App 1a. Double click on Cytoscape icon 1b. Open EnrichmentMap App In the Cytoscape top menu bar: Click on Apps -> EnrichmentMap A ‘Create Enrichment Map’ window is now opened. Step 2 Create an enrichment map from the UP and DOWN g:Profiler result files. 2a. In the ‘Create Enrichment Map’ window, drag and drop the 2 enrichment files enrichment_results_gprofiler_UPgenes.gem.txt and enrichment_results_gprofiler_DNgenes.gem.txt. 2b. In the white box, click on “enrichment_results_gprofiler_UPgenes (Generic/gProfiler)” 2c. On the right side, go to the GMT field, click on the 3 radio button (…) and locate the file gprofiler_full_hsapiens.name.gmt that you have saved on your computer to upload it. 2d. In the white box, click on “enrichment_results_gprofiler_DNgenes (Generic/gProfiler)” 2e. On the right side, go to the GMT field, click on the 3 radio button (…) and locate the file gprofiler_full_hsapiens.name.gmt that you have saved on your computer to upload it. 2f. Locate the FDR q-value cutoff field and set the value to 0.01 2g. Select the Connectivity slide bar to sparse. Instead of specifying the gmt file for each dataset separately, if all the datasets in your analysis use the same gmt file, you can specify a common gmt file to be used by all datasets. Click +Add… and select Add Common Files On the right side, go to the GMT file field, click on the 3 radio button (…) and locate the file gprofiler_full_hsapiens.name.gmt that you have saved on your computer to upload it. This can also be done for a shared expression file. 2h. Click on Build. If you have specified common files this info box will appear * Click on Continue to build A status bar should pop up showing progress of the Enrichment map build. There might be multiple messages that appear when you first create an enrichment map. You can choose to silence them if you want (Although the yfiles message will continue to appear every two weeks). * Click on OK * Click on OK Step 3: Explore the results: In the EnrichmentMap control panel located at the left: Select the 2 Data Sets (checked by default) Set Chart Data to Color by Data Set Select Publication Ready to remove gene-set label to have a global view of the map. un-select Publication Ready when you explore the map in more detail to see the gene-set names. On the map, a node that is coloured both green and blue is a gene-set that is found in both the UP and DOWN g:Profiler result sets. A node that is blue is a gene-set that is found only in the DOWN-regulated results (enrichment_results_gprofiler_DNgenes). A node that is green is a gene-set that is found only in the UP-regulated results (enrichment_results_gprofiler_UPgenes). A blue edge represents genes that overlap between gene-sets found in the DOWN-regulated results. A green edge represents genes that overlap between gene-sets found in the UP-regulated results. Are there pathways enriched in both the UP and DOWN gene lists? What might this mean biologically? Explore Detailed results In the Cytoscape menu bar, select ‘View” and ’Show Graphic Details’ to display node labels. Make sure you have unselected “Publication Ready” in the EnrichmentMap control panel. Zoom in to be able to read the labels and navigate the network using the bird eye view (blue rectangle). Select a node and visualize the Table Panel Click on a node For this example the node “MET_activates” has been selected. you can type it in the search bar, quotes are important. When the node is selected, it is highlighted in yellow. In table panel, we can see the genes included in the gene-set. A green colored box indicates that the gene is in the gene-set(pathway) and in our gene list. A gray colored box indicated that the gene is in the gene-set but not in our gene list. Equivalent RCy3 code — Exercise 1a: Build EM from UP and DOWN g:Profiler results # Upload GEM files to Cytoscape up_gem_cyto <- upload_em_file(up_gem) dn_gem_cyto <- upload_em_file(dn_gem) gmt_cyto <- upload_em_file(gmt_baderlab) # Build the EnrichmentMap with both datasets em1a_command <- paste( "enrichmentmap build", "analysisType=generic", paste0("enrichmentsDataset1=", up_gem_cyto), paste0("gmtFile=", gmt_cyto), paste0("enrichmentsDataset2=", dn_gem_cyto), "qvalue=0.01", "pvalue=1.0", "coefficients=JACCARD", "similaritycutoff=0.35", sep = " " ) commandsRun(em1a_command, base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) # Get the newly created network em1a_suid <- getNetworkSuid(base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) message("Exercise 1a EM SUID: ", em1a_suid) existing_names <- getNetworkList(base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) new_name <- "EM_UP_vs_DN_gprofiler" if (new_name %in% existing_names) { new_name <- paste0(sample(1000:9999, 2),"_",new_name ) } renameNetwork(new_name, network = getNetworkSuid(base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl), base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) message("Network renamed to: ", new_name) # Apply a layout layoutNetwork("force-directed defaultSpringCoefficient=0.00004 defaultSpringLength=5", network = em1a_suid, base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) # Search for a specific node (e.g. "MET activates") and select it selectNodes(nodes = "MET ACTIVATES PTK2 SIGNALING%REACTOME DATABASE ID RELEASE 97%8874081", by.col = "name", network = em1a_suid, base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) # View the node table for the selected node selected_node_table <- getTableColumns( table = "node", network = em1a_suid, base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl ) # Filter to the selected node selected_nodes <- getSelectedNodes(network = em1a_suid, base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) print(selected_node_table[selected_node_table$name %in% selected_nodes, ]) Exercise 1b - create EM from fgsea results using Baderlab genesets Create an enrichment map from fgsea results run using the custom Baderlab gene-set file. Using a pre-filtered pathway database (max 250 genes per set) means the FDR is calculated only on these gene-sets, giving a more focused and interpretable result compared to filtering after the fact. For this exercise, we will use: fgsea result file: fgsea_report_for_list.tsv Filtered gmt file: Human_GOBP_AllPathways_filtered_500orLessV2.gmt. To create an enrichment map of these results: Go to Control Panel and select the EnrichmentMap tab. Click on the “+” sign to re-open the Create Enrichment Map window. Click on Reset to reset the Enrichment map panel Drag the fgsea GEM file fgsea_report_for_list.tsv and the filtered gmt file Human_GOBP_AllPathways_filtered_500orLessV2.gmt into the Datasets box on Enrichment map panel. In the white box, select the “fgsea_resistant_vs_parental (Generic/gProfiler)” file Locate the GMT field and upload the file “Human_GOBP_AllPathways_filtered_500orLessV2.gmt”. Set the FDR q-value cutoff to 0.01 and set the Connectivity slide bar to second level. Explore the results: SAVE YOUR CYTOSCAPE SESSION (.cys) FILE ! Equivalent RCy3 code — Exercise 1b: Build EM from fgsea results with Baderlab GMT # Upload the fgsea GEM and Baderlab GMT to Cytoscape fgsea_gem_cyto <- upload_em_file(fgsea_gem) rnk_cyto <- upload_em_file(rnk_file) gmt_bader_cyto <- upload_em_file(gmt_baderlab) # Build the EnrichmentMap from fgsea results em1b_command <- paste( "enrichmentmap build", "analysisType=GSEA", paste0("enrichmentsDataset1=", fgsea_gem_cyto), paste0("gmtFile=", gmt_bader_cyto), paste0("ranksDataset1=", rnk_cyto), "qvalue=0.05", "pvalue=1.0", "coefficients=COMBINED", "similaritycutoff=0.5", # second-level connectivity sep = " " ) commandsRun(em1b_command, base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) existing_names <- getNetworkList(base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) new_name <- "EM_fgsea_Baderlab" if (new_name %in% existing_names) { new_name <- paste0(sample(1000:9999, 2),"_",new_name ) } renameNetwork(new_name, network = getNetworkSuid(base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl), base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) message("Network renamed to: ", new_name) em1b_suid <- getNetworkSuid(base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) message("Exercise 1b fgsea EM SUID: ", em1b_suid) layoutNetwork("force-directed defaultSpringCoefficient=0.00004 defaultSpringLength=5", network = em1b_suid, base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) # Save the Cytoscape session saveSession(filename = file.path(path_to_save_cytoscape,"module9_gprofiler_session.cys"), base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) message("Session saved.") Exercise 1c (optional) - investigate individual pathways in GeneMANIA or String ** This requires that you install additional Cytoscape Apps - GeneMania and String ** Each node in the Enrichment map represents a biological process or pathway. It consists of a collection of genes. Often we want to know how the genes in that group interact. There are many different ways you can investigate the underlying interactions for the given group. Some involve searching online databases and others are directly integrated into cytoscape. GeneMANIA - an integrative database of gene connections including co-expression, protein interactions, genetic interactions, pathways and more. Cytoscape App String - an integrative database of gene connections including co-expression, protein interactions, genetic interactions, pathways and more. Cytoscape App Pathway Commons - a intergrative database of pathways. (There is a beta feature in EM to show your pathway in the painter app, a pathway common web page that overlays your expression data on the given pathway. Still in beta testing and requires expression data to work correctly so won’t work for this example) GeneMANIA Navigate to the enrichment map that you created using the fgsea Baderlab results (Exercise 1b) Click on Network Tab and navigate to the third network (it should be the third network if you followed the above examples - name: fgsea_resistant_vs_parental_gem) or in the Enrichment map panel in the top drop down select the network named fgsea_resistant_vs_parental_gem In the cytoscape search bar enter “MET activates” If you can’t see the selected nodes, click on “Fit Selected” to focus on the selected node. Right click on the node “MET activates” and Select Apps –> Enrichmemt Map - Show in GeneMANIA A GeneMANIA Query Panel will pop up. Select Select leading edge to reduce the query set to just the genes found to influence the expression of this pathway. Click on OK A GeneMANIA network will show up with the connections between the genes found in your query set and the pathway “MET activates” We will go more in depth into GeneMANIA in module 5 Equivalent RCy3 code — Exercise 1c: Select a node and query GeneMANIA via the command interface Caveat - there is no way to selected just the leading edge through RCy3 because it is a functionality that is only present in the interface. The network you get from code will be larger. # Navigate to the fgsea EM network setCurrentNetwork(network = em1b_suid, base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) # Select the "MET activates" node selectNodes(nodes = "MET ACTIVATES PTK2 SIGNALING%REACTOME DATABASE ID RELEASE 97%8874081", by.col = "name", network = em1b_suid, base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) # Fit the view to the selected node fitContent(selected.only = TRUE, base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) # Get the genes in this pathway from the node table node_tbl <- getTableColumns(table = "node", network = em1b_suid, base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) met_row <- node_tbl[grepl("MET activates", node_tbl$name, ignore.case = TRUE), ] # The EnrichmentMap::Genes column holds the genes in the leading edge / # gene-set intersection — extract them to use as the GeneMANIA query met_genes <- unlist(met_row[["EnrichmentMap::Genes"]][1]) met_genes <- met_genes[met_genes != ""] message("Genes in 'met activates': ", paste(met_genes, collapse = ", ")) # Query GeneMANIA via its Cytoscape app command # (requires GeneMANIA Cytoscape app to be installed) genemania_command <- paste0( "genemania search genes=\"", paste(met_genes, collapse = "|"), "\" organism=Homo sapiens" ) commandsRun(genemania_command, base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) String Navigate to the enrichment map that you created using the fgsea Baderlab results (Exercise 1b) Click on Network Tab and navigate to the third network (it should be the third network if you followed the above examples - name: fgsea_resistant_vs_parental_gem) or in the Enrichment map panel in the top drop down select the network named fgsea_resistant_vs_parental_gem In the cytoscape search bar enter “MET activates” If you can’t see the selected nodes, click on “Fit Selected” to focus on the selected node. Right click on the node “MET activates” and Select Apps –> Enrichmemt Map - Show in String A String Query Panel will pop up. Select Select genes with expression to reduce the query set to just the genes in the given that pathway that was in your original dataset (for example we search for a set of 127 genes in g:profiler but the given pathway has 233 genes associated with it of which only 10 genes are found in our original query set ) Click on OK A String network will show up with the connections between the genes found in your query set and the pathway “MET activates” Equivalent RCy3 code — Exercise 1c: Query String for genes in a selected pathway Caveat - there is no way to selected just the leading edge through RCy3 because it is a functionality that is only present in the interface. The network you get from code will be larger. # Using the met_genes vector extracted above, query String via its app command # (requires STRINGapp Cytoscape app to be installed) string_command <- paste0( "string protein query", " query=\"", paste(met_genes, collapse = ","), "\"", " species=\"Homo sapiens\"", " limit=0", # only return queried proteins, no additional interactors " cutoff=0.4" ) commandsRun(string_command, base.url = current_cytoscape_baseurl) Explore the features and data of each Cytoscape app.What sort of information does each tell you?
